agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.mechanism: Drought kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.conditionality: This is an establishment-phase risk first, which is the phase a project funds and is exposed to: the measured damage falls mostly on seedlings and newly planted trees [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5], though established cabruca cocoa and its shade trees also died in the El Niño drought [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2]. Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The cocoa units are crop-specific and enter the row under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, with no measured damage, so it does not show the system is undamaged by extreme rainfall [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of rainstorm damage would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.mechanism: Accidental fire can damage trees and crops in silvopastoral and agrosilvopastoral systems, and post-fire re-establishment costs could be high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. In Senegal, fire is named among the causes of failed regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, together with grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots, climate change and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.conditionality: The literature units are statements rather than measurements: the Brazilian unit reports a cited author's comment on producer concern, and the Senegalese unit lists fire among several regeneration threats [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The literature sources are upper-middle-income Brazil and lower-middle-income Senegal [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.mechanism: Flooding and increased runoff from heavier rainfall could increase soil nutrient loss and erosion within tropical agroforestry systems, and flooding increases tree mortality in cacao agroforests, with older systems potentially more vulnerable [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.conditionality: The literature units are a tropics review reading earlier studies second-hand; the erosion statement is forward-looking and concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding, a no-damage finding for that crop [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2]. The coping ratings are practitioner judgements on technology sheets, not measured damage [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood]. Burkina Faso is low income and Kenya and India lower-middle income [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood, ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.mechanism: The IPCC assessment states that climate change affects agroforestry productivity much as it does individual perennial crops, through increased temperature or water stress, more crop pathogens, changes in pollinator abundance and changes in nutrient content [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one assessment statement that bundles several climate pressures rather than heat alone, notes limited research on tree crops, reports no measured damage, and records no country or income group [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1]. A second independent source or one measured finding of heat damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.mechanism: A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The damage findings are second-hand: the hurricane result is cited, compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and names no location, and the seedling unit lists wind among several establishment-phase needs alongside trampling, herbivory, weeds and fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. Against them, the only measured unit, in shaded coffee in Chiapas, Mexico, found minimal vegetation damage from the hurricane, though the unit records its winds as mild [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]; a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]; and the Burkina Faso rating is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. Burkina Faso is low income, India lower-middle and Brazil and Mexico upper-middle income [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.mechanism: Trees kept in or added to farmland hold more species than the treeless or simplified land use they replace. Pooled over 47 publications, silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures; systems with native, unplanted trees were 36.3% above open pasture against 20.9% for planted systems, and invertebrate biodiversity in native-tree systems was 53.7% above open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. For coffee and cacao, a global meta-analysis (De Beenhouwer et al. 2013) found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest was compared with sparse-shade plantation, because the diverse, structurally complex shade canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems (Gordon et al. 2007) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Across tropical agroforestry interventions, natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant than in the same crop without trees [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. In a ten-year trial on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, earthworm diversity (Simpson's index) was 0.62 in a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems are reported, citing earlier studies, to carry four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures and 62% higher ant species richness than treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]; a World Bank silvopastoral operation reported increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; and silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and the Kenyan WOCAT compiler notes that FMNR sites provide more habitats than degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica see live fences as corridors for fauna and flora [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.conditionality: The gains are measured against degraded, treeless or simplified baselines (open pasture, monoculture, sparse-shade plantation, degraded sites). Against natural forest the same coffee and cacao meta-analysis found agroforest held 11% fewer species in total and 35% fewer forest species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4], and silvopasture with native trees held 18.1% lower biodiversity than native forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]; these mark a ceiling rather than a loss caused by the practice, which replaces farmland, not forest. The other harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while yields of about 750 kg/ha were possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Not every measure rises: in the pest-control meta-analysis most studies found no effect of agroforestry on the diversity of natural enemies, and predation and parasitism responses were mixed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2], and the invertebrate-abundance response in native-tree silvopasture was not statistically significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. Design and species matter: a review notes the benefit depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3], and among coffee certification schemes in Nicaragua C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one under which tree diversity fell [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The class is set by a vote across sub-practices, which lands on a moderate increase although shaded perennial and planted silvoarable systems on their own reach strong. Several units are second-hand readings or practitioner ratings, the deforestation finding gives a direction with no size and counts as a component of biodiversity rather than a measure of it, and the silvopasture meta-analysis does not name its study countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific; the low- and lower-middle-income fit rests on Niger, Kenya, India, Nicaragua, Cameroon and the cocoa meta-analysis's mainly lower-middle-income studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.mechanism: A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee and cocoa reports, from a meta-analysis of 74 studies, a stronger decline in total species richness from agroforestry to plantations (−46%) than from forest to agroforestry (−11%), and, from another study, bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.conditionality: The shaded-coffee and cocoa review figures are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and the review notes the shaded systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. The harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The richness drop from forest to agroforestry (−11%) marks that shaded systems hold less than forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1]. All units are crop-specific coffee or cocoa; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries, while the review's studies are not assigned a country [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. The Kenyan WOCAT compiler rates animal and habitat diversity as increased on FMNR sites, noting that many animal species find safe habitats there and that FMNR sites provide more habitats than degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. A meta-analysis of cocoa, drawing mainly on lower-middle-income countries, found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and in Nicaraguan coffee most certification schemes had positive impacts on a tree diversity index used as a proxy for habitat quality [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The harm finding in this row is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Among the Nicaraguan schemes, C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one with a negative impact on tree diversity, and that finding is read second-hand [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The Kenyan units are compiler ratings against degraded sites rather than species surveys, and the Niger result counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. No unit gives a size for the gain in animal or habitat diversity.

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report attributes increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species, to silvopastoral systems at farm and landscape level [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], and in the Colombian Amazon piedmont silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The Colombian project evaluations give no effect sizes, and the deforestation result enters as a forest-cover component rather than a measured biodiversity outcome [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia only. The Colombian bird and ant figures are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Trees added to cropland and pasture store carbon in their biomass and soil, and the row's class rests on the evidence that sets that storage against the other greenhouse gases. A global synthesis combining carbon sequestration in biomass and soil with changes in net methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions estimated that a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 (± 13.5) t CO2 eq per hectare a year, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. In Colombia, a preliminary balance by Naranjo et al. (2012), cited in a Spanish-language review, found that in intensive silvopastoral systems lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture offset the methane emitted by the cattle [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. The storage evidence itself is large and consistent in direction. A global meta-analysis found agroforestry systems stored an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8) in tree biomass and increased soil organic carbon stocks by an average of 25.9% (17.4–34.4%), with a greater gain where trees were established in cropland than in pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2]; another put soil carbon stocks under agroforestry at 126 Mg C·ha−1, 19% more than in cropland or pasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]; and the global synthesis reports soil carbon sequestration between about 0.5 and 2 t C per hectare a year at sites less than 10 years old, with none of the compiled studies reporting carbon losses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kim16_1]. IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates between 0.59 and 6.24 t ha–1 yr–1 of carbon above-ground at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and describe large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures in sub-Saharan Africa (RR 1.2), the tropics (overall effect size 1.21) and West African fields with shrubs and trees (+ 20 to 75%) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]; a global synthesis for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1]. In shaded tree crops, total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in a monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], a coffee agroforestry farm in Costa Rica stored a mean 3.6 t C/ha/yr over eight years of eddy-covariance measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rican silvopasture, carbon storage potential was 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1 against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12], and the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler notes that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in Colombia, compared with control properties, enters as a forest-cover component with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: Only the net balances set the class; the many carbon-storage figures (biomass and soil stocks, sequestration rates, IPCC potentials, project totals) are carried and described but held out, because they count carbon removals without the methane and nitrous oxide that a change of land use can also shift [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4]. Those other gases do not move one way: the global synthesis found inconsistent changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions with conversion from agriculture to agroforestry, with no clear direction of change, though net soil CH4 rose with a change to shaded perennial-crop systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. The net estimate covers young systems only, and the Colombian balance is preliminary and reaches this row second-hand from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]; that is why the class is slight and its strength not quantified, not because storage is small. The starting land use decides the sign of the soil side: converting forest to agroforestry gave a stock change factor of 0.89, a soil carbon loss, and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry (0.23 t C ha−1 yr−1) was not significantly different from zero [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]; a global meta-analysis likewise found that conversion from pastures to agroforestry did not affect soil organic carbon stocks, while conversion from cropland generally increased them [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3], and silvopasture had the lowest increase or even no change in soil carbon stocks because topsoil carbon there is driven by grass inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. Measured on-farm comparisons also sit close to no effect in places: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; in Niger, after four years, the block with Ziziphus held 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua showed gains in above-ground carbon stocks that were not statistically significant [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. Much of the storage evidence is assessment-level or modelled (global technical and economic potentials, per-hectare mitigation densities), and the project totals carry no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]; the IPCC notes regional estimates are scant and options differ by geography [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_7]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement, not a measured stock [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Coffee, cocoa and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1]. What would strengthen the class is more whole-system greenhouse-gas balances, carbon stored net of methane and nitrous oxide, for established systems in LIC/LMIC settings. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Trees on rainfed cropland add carbon to the soil, mainly under their canopies, through litter and root inputs on soils depleted by annual cropping. A meta-analysis of semi-arid West Africa found that shrubs and trees on agricultural fields raised soil total carbon by 20 to 75%, an effect ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping under the canopies of woody perennials [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil organic carbon storage [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. An FAO review for Senegal cites a meta-analysis by Sileshi (2016) that soil under the canopy of Faidherbia albida holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than soil outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. In a 10-year field experiment on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon reached 0.59% under a Gmelina–mango–pigeon pea system against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from 0.30% at the start [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. In southern Malawi, soil carbon showed a trend upward with a Tephrosia relay intercrop, 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: Not every field trial finds the gain. In Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, soil organic carbon did not significantly differ under and outside the canopy of Faidherbia albida at the end of the 2013 season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1], and in Niger, after four years, the block with Ziziphus trees held 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. What separates the results, as far as the evidence says, is time and where the carbon is measured: the large gains are under canopies or after a decade of tree growth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1], while the null results come from single seasons or a few years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Under-canopy figures do not scale to the whole field: the parkland comparisons set soil under the tree against soil outside it, so the field-level gain depends on how much of the field the canopies cover [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The evidence is soil carbon only, a component of carbon removals; it does not add up storage in tree biomass, and the West African meta-analysis reports ranges across studies rather than a pooled effect [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]. The global meta-analysis also found that converting pasture rather than cropland to agroforestry did not affect soil carbon stocks, so the gain applies to cropland conversion [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading of Sileshi (2016) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. Most of the evidence is from low- and lower-middle-income West Africa, Ethiopia, Malawi and India, within the LIC/LMIC target. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Spanish-language reviews report that intensive silvopastoral systems capture more carbon, offsetting livestock methane, that silvopastoral systems established from degraded natural woodland increase above- and below-ground carbon stocks, and that in a Colombian climate-smart prioritisation only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: All three are cited secondary statements without effect sizes; among them an expert prioritisation matrix rather than a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. They come from Colombia and Latin America generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Shade and timber trees in tree-crop systems add biomass carbon over the crop alone. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry, including cocoa and shade trees, is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance of trees, coffee, litter and soil gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. East African perennial tree-crop systems hold 29.9 Mg C ha−1 of above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4], and modelled Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee systems translate to biomass carbon of 139.5 and 153.4 Mg/ha [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. A coffee review reports agroforestry can improve soil organic matter by 20–35% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The soil side is weaker than the biomass side: the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1], and the coffee soil figure is a review's second-hand reading [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5]. The Costa Rican coffee units are from a high-income country, and the shaded-coffee figure is cited from earlier work [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]; the Ethiopian figures are model outputs cited second-hand [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The East African and Ethiopian figures are stocks, not annual rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4]. Coffee, cocoa and enset units are crop-specific; the low- and lower-middle-income fit rests on the cocoa meta-analysis and the East African review [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance of trees, coffee, litter and soil gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29.8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: These units come from high-income Costa Rica, from coffee and silvopastoral systems, and the shaded-coffee and silvopasture figures are cited secondary results [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. They lie outside the LIC/LMIC target income band and should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems without local evidence [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, trees on farms raise both biomass and soil carbon. Across sub-Saharan Africa, agroforestry improved soil organic carbon over controls (RR 1.2) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]; in West African fields, the presence of shrubs and trees raised soil total C overall, though variably (+ 20 to 75%), ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]; and a meta-analysis cited for Senegal reports 46 per cent more soil organic carbon under Faidherbia canopy than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil, with much of the above-ground carbon held in homegardens, perennial tree-crop systems and trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5]. On degraded lateritic soils in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system raised soil organic carbon to 0.59% after 10 years, against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12]. A multi-country restoration programme observed an overall relative increase of 3% in soil organic carbon over baseline and a significant association between scaling up trees on-farm and gains in soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_4]. Modelled regional potentials put agroforestry at 0.19 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Africa and the Middle East and 0.37 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Asia and the developing Pacific at up to $100/tCO2eq [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: On-farm measurements are mixed: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; at Sadore in Niger, soil cropped with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held 5 to 10% more soil organic carbon than soil cropped without them, but the difference was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; cocoa agroforestry showed no significant differences in soil chemical properties from monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua had positive but not statistically significant impacts on above-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. The programme's 3% gain varied significantly across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2]. Several units are stocks rather than annual rates, the Ethiopian project totals carry no per-hectare denominator, and the regional potentials are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. The pooled size rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component of sequestration [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is a compiler judgement, not a measured stock [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Coffee, cocoa, coconut and enset units are crop-specific [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kumar22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Trees added to cropland or pasture remove carbon from the air and store it in two places: in standing tree biomass and in the soil. On the biomass side, a global meta-analysis of tree-based agroforestry (windbreaks, alley cropping, hedgerows, shelterbelts, silvopasture) found the systems stored an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8) in tree biomass, against adjacent cropland or pasture with no trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1]. On the soil side, the same meta-analysis found agroforestry raised soil organic carbon stocks by an average of 25.9% (17.4–34.4%), with the larger gain where trees were established in cropland [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]; a second meta-analysis found soil carbon stocks under agroforestry of 126 Mg C·ha−1, 19% more than in cropland or pasture, driven by litter from tree pruning and root inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]; and the IPCC Tier 1 revision put the soil carbon stock change factor for cropland converted to agroforestry at 1.25 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: What the land was before decides whether soil carbon storage rises. Converting cropland adds soil carbon, but converting pasture did not change soil carbon stocks in one meta-analysis, because perennial grass already supplies large below-ground carbon inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4]; silvopasture had the lowest increase or no change against nearby pasture in another [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]; and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry was not significantly different from zero (0.23±0.25 t C ha−1 yr−1) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. The harm finding is a conversion from forest: the IPCC Tier 1 revision gives a stock change factor of 0.89 for forests converted to agroforestry, so clearing forest for agroforestry loses soil carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2]; that is the existing-forest baseline, not the farmland the practice is meant to replace. The biomass figure is a stock that rises with tree age toward an equilibrium, not an annual removal rate, and none of these units is a net greenhouse-gas balance [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1]. All units are global meta-analyses pooled across income groups and climates with no country list in the text, which is why this row is scoped to mixed income contexts; the shift of the class to LIC/LMIC settings rests on that pooling [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Colombian project measurements attribute net CO2 removals to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences and intensive silvopasture, and a preliminary balance reports that greater carbon capture and lower nitrogen losses in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in the Colombian Amazon piedmont, compared with control properties, also enters as a forest-cover component, with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A global modelling study finds that the highest cost-effective mitigation potential in Eastern Europe and West-Central Asia comes from agroforestry (0.18 GtCO2eq yr−1; 24%) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_5].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The Colombian figure is a project total with no per-hectare or per-year denominator, and the preliminary balance is a cited secondary result without a usable rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. The regional figure is modelled, not measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_5]. The field evidence comes from livestock systems in upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].

agroforestry__catchment_water_yield.mechanism: Trees change how much rain reaches groundwater and streams in opposite ways. On the recharge side, the IPCC assessment states that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], and, combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, Ilstedt et al. derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. On the water-use side, a review cites Wallace et al. (2005): because agroforestry systems include a share of trees, they use more water than pure agricultural systems, though less than full-cover forest, leaving less water to feed groundwater and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. Groundwater recharge is used here as a component of catchment water yield.
agroforestry__catchment_water_yield.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is the balance between higher tree water use and better infiltration, which tree density sets. The recharge gains are qualified to moderate density and to an optimal intermediate density in dryland parklands, so the benefit does not keep rising with tree cover [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]; the loss rests on the general point that more trees transpire more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. The recharge statements are about drylands, while the water-use statement is general, so the row cannot say which side wins in a given catchment. All units are second-hand readings in reviews or assessments, the recharge units rest on the same primary work by Ilstedt et al., none states a size or a country, and no unit measures water leaving a catchment or reaching downstream users [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6, ev_water_yield_zhu19_1].

agroforestry__cost_per_beneficiary.mechanism: A programme cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices cost $66 per household in Ghana, where the practice was farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR), and $201 per household in Rwanda, where it was tree-planting agroforestry [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. The denominator is each household adopting at least one land restoration practice [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3].
agroforestry__cost_per_beneficiary.conditionality: The two figures are arms of one programme with different practices and countries (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income), inside the LIC/LMIC target, and the source links the lower Ghana cost to FMNR versus tree planting where household land is more limited [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. They are programme expenditure levels, not cost changes against a control, and with one source and two arms they do not pool into a range [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

agroforestry__cost_per_hectare_restored.mechanism: The same programme reports $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana and $1,387 per hectare for tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda, counted per hectare where at least one land restoration practice is adopted [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4].
agroforestry__cost_per_hectare_restored.conditionality: The two figures are arms of one programme that differ widely by practice and country (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income), so they describe two different costs rather than one pooled range [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. They are programme expenditure levels, not costs relative to a control [ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__cost_per_tco2e_avoided.mechanism: The IPCC land report states that the cost of agroforestry as a response option is less than 10 USD per tonne CO2e, among the lower-cost options, against as much as 250 USD for BECCS [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4].
agroforestry__cost_per_tco2e_avoided.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class for this cell: it is one global upper-bound statement citing an earlier assessment, with no country, income group, currency year or practice detail, and the source adds that economic barriers other than cost may prevent implementation [ev_project_cost_ipccsrccl6_4]. A second independent source or one measured cost per tonne from a project would let the cell state a class.

agroforestry__cost_reduction.mechanism: Trees change farm costs in both directions, mostly through labour. Some systems save cost: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, an estimate from a Bank-commissioned business case attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. Others add cost: in the forest zone of Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 (38%) person-days per hectare per year and variable costs by 34% averaged over the trial, for hedgerow planting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]; and at Ibadan, Nigeria, maize mulched with cut-and-carry tree leaves needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, with 96% of the labour going to collecting and managing the mulch and only 4% to weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].
agroforestry__cost_reduction.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is where the trees' labour falls. Where the trees grow in the field and suppress weeds, as the Rwandan Tephrosia did, weeding labour falls [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]; where tree biomass must be pruned, cut and carried, the extra handling outweighs the weeding saved, and in Nigeria the mulch was grown on a separate plot and carried in [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Between them sit no-change findings: A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies in low- and middle-income countries reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952), with an interval spanning a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), pooling agroforestry applied alone or in bundles [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The Cameroon costs mix establishment and recurrent pruning labour, and its trees were pruned only from the second year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Colombian figure is a modelled recurrent saving from an upper-middle-income country and does not pool with the relative changes [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. The coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. The field evidence is otherwise from low-income Rwanda and lower-middle-income Cameroon and Nigeria, within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1, ev_project_cost_korm99_4].

agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.mechanism: Trees in rainfed cropland raise labour costs rather than lowering them. In Cameroon, averaged over 3 years and taking the traditional maize/groundnut system as the reference, planting Leucaena hedgerows raised variable costs by 34%, and labour rose from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare per year, for hedgerow establishment, cutting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In south-western Nigeria, maize mulched with leaves cut and carried from multipurpose trees needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, and with Gliricidia sepium or Senna siamea mulch 96% of the total labour went on collecting and managing the mulch [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.conditionality: Both units are research-managed trials in the sub-humid and humid tropics of West and Central Africa, lower-middle-income settings. The higher costs bought higher returns in Cameroon, where unfertilised alley cropping gave the highest net benefit, so cost here is not the same as net loss [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Where labour or land is scarce, the extra labour can make the practice unattractive [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].

agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.mechanism: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__farming_sy.conditionality: The evidence is thin, so confidence is low and no cost class is set. The Rwandan saving is a labour figure from a small on-farm trial, and Tephrosia there is a cut-back mulch shrub rather than a shade tree, so it says little about the cost of shade-tree systems [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. The cocoa meta-analysis finds no cost difference, and its costs are annual production costs that in some studies include certification or land rent [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. Both units are crop-specific (coffee or cocoa) and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; the evidence is from low- and lower-middle-income producers.

agroforestry__cost_reduction__income_gro.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, the evidence finds agroforestry costs sometimes lower, sometimes higher and sometimes unchanged, depending on what the trees do to the farm's labour. Where the trees replace a task, labour falls: in Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia intercropping required 30 man-days per hectare less than current farmer management because less weeding was needed [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. Where the trees add a task, labour rises: in Nigerian maize, plots mulched with tree prunings needed more labour than the fertilizer and untreated controls, with 96% of the labour spent collecting and managing mulch and only 4% weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]; and in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%) and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Pooled studies sit between: a meta-analysis of field studies reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952) [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1], and a cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__cost_reduction__income_gro.conditionality: The studies disagree, so no direction is stated. What separates them is the labour the trees bring: the saving comes with a weed-suppressing intercrop in an established tree crop [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3], while the cost rises come with cut-and-carry mulching and hedgerow pruning in annual maize systems, where cutting, carrying and spreading prunings is the added work [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and fell from the first to the third year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The pooled meta-analysis interval spans both a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), its table pools observations where agroforestry was applied alone or in bundles with other practices, and the costs are mostly variable rather than establishment costs [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The cocoa unit is crop-specific and draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. For a project, labour demand at planting and pruning, and whether it falls in seasonal peaks, is the cost question to check.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: One tropics review, citing earlier studies, reports that severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3], and that another study found drought exposure did not increase seedling mortality, despite impaired growth [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: both units come from one review reading other studies second-hand, they point in different directions, and none is a measured finding of the review itself; no country or income group is recorded [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. A second independent source or one measured finding of drought damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: A systematic review reports, second-hand, a hypothetical study in Hawaii finding that the flammability of tropical agroforestry systems is likely not to be affected by increasing temperatures (+2°C) [ev_fire_hazard_watts22_15].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one modelled statement from a high-income US setting outside the LIC/LMIC target, and it concerns how warming changes flammability, not how much damage fire does to trees when it occurs [ev_fire_hazard_watts22_15]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: One tropics review, citing earlier studies, states that flooding and increased runoff from heavier rainfall could increase soil nutrient loss and erosion within tropical agroforestry systems [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single forward-looking statement read second-hand, it concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and no country or income group is recorded [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13]. A second independent source or one measured finding of flood damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: Climate change affects agroforestry productivity much as it does individual perennial crops, through increased temperature or water stress, more crop pathogens, changes in pollinator abundance and changes in nutrient content [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: This IPCC assessment statement covers several climate pressures at once, not heat alone, and notes there is little research on tree crops [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1]. It is global, with no country or income group recorded [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.mechanism: A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8].
agroforestry__cross_family__asset_threat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one study read second-hand, it compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and the citing passage names no location [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind or cyclone damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__cross_family__biodiversity.mechanism: A review of nature-based solutions states that agroforestry is likely to have biodiversity benefits compared with conventional arable, pasture or forestry land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of agroforestry against the same crops grown without trees found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__biodiversity.conditionality: More enemies is not the same as more kinds of enemy: in the same meta-analysis the majority of studies (7 out of 11) showed no effect of agroforestry on enemy diversity, and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. The benefit therefore rests on abundance of a functional group, not on species richness. The review makes the benefit depend on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used, and its statement is a synthesis of a cited European meta-analysis carrying no effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. Neither source states how large the gain is, so the strength is not quantified. The meta-analysis is almost entirely tropical (shaded coffee, cocoa and plantain, alley cropping and improved fallows, with maize the commonest crop), the closer match to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__carbon_seque.mechanism: IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates above-ground carbon at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and the SRCCL describes large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses in sub-Saharan Africa and the humid tropics report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures, used here as the soil-carbon component, and East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1]. A global synthesis built for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean soil organic carbon stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. Global meta-analyses comparing agroforestry with adjacent cropland or pasture find carbon removals in both biomass and soil: tree biomass held an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8), soil organic carbon stocks rose by an average of 25.9%, with a greater gain where trees were established in cropland rather than pasture, and a separate synthesis found soil carbon stocks 19% higher, driven by litter from tree pruning and root inputs [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]. A further global synthesis estimated that a shift to agroforestry, counting biomass and soil carbon together with changes in soil methane and nitrous oxide, can mitigate 27.2 t CO2 eq per hectare per year over the early growth stage, up to an average age of 14 years; none of its compiled studies reported soil carbon losses, but soil stocks rise at a diminishing rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kim16_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__carbon_seque.conditionality: Much of the evidence is assessment-level or cited-secondary, including global technical and economic potentials and modelled per-hectare densities [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1]. The pooled magnitude rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component rather than a sequestration rate; the Regreening Africa endline found only a small relative soil-carbon increase with large variation across sites, and the IPCC notes that regional estimates are scant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_7]. The starting land use decides the sign: converting forest to agroforestry gave a stock change factor of 0.89, a soil carbon loss, and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry (0.23 t C ha−1 yr−1) was not significantly different from zero [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. The same synthesis found inconsistent changes in net methane and nitrous oxide emissions after conversion to agroforestry, with no clear direction, so the climate benefit rests on carbon storage rather than on lower emissions of those gases [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_3]. The class stays slight because the cross-family evidence does not settle a size that holds across sub-practices and starting land uses: the global figures pool very different systems, and the per-year rate covers only the early growth stage [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__catchment_wa.mechanism: Trees both add and use water in a catchment, and the evidence here shows each pathway once. A review of agroforestry water and soil losses states, citing Wallace et al. (2005), that because agroforestry systems include a proportion of trees they use more water than pure agricultural systems (though less than a full-cover forest), leaving less water to feed groundwater bodies and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__catchment_wa.conditionality: The sources point in opposite directions, so the row states no direction. What separates them, as far as the evidence says, is tree density and the balance between tree water use and the water trees let into the soil: the recharge gain is qualified to moderate density in drylands [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], while the loss is the general case of trees using more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. agroforestry__cross_family__production_g.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of agroforestry adoption by smallholders in sub-Saharan Africa found a significant yield gain for maize in the high-quality studies (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42), and a pan-tropical meta-analysis of pest control reports that the only studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found a gain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2, ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__production_g.conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, the sub-Saharan adoption meta-analysis found that agroforestry overall is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1], an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with an even split of gains and losses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13].

agroforestry__cross_family__rural_povert.mechanism: An East African systematic review counts income among the main livelihood benefits of agroforestry, diversifying rural livelihoods and acting as a safety net in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_household_income_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report favourable financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of sub-Saharan adoption studies, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, found agroforestry adoption raises household income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001), from diversified revenue in fruit, timber and fuelwood [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, cash-crop revenues, especially from cardamom, and total income were significantly higher on farms using improved agroforestry, and gross income per capita was US$ 157 against US$ 74 on traditional farms [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In West Java, Indonesia, agroforestry had a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than swidden cultivation, according to a review's reading of Rahman et al. (2017) [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].
agroforestry__cross_family__rural_povert.conditionality: Several units show no effect or a loss: the pooled systematic-review income effect is not statistically significant, Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged and no short-term income change detectable, and some Brazilian system components were loss-making [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. The working paper's revenue measure is gross revenue, not profit, and not significant [ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Mozambique result is a review citation without an effect size [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The sub-Saharan pooled income effect rests on adopter versus non-adopter contrasts, many with weak causal identification, and its pool includes payments for ecosystem services in Mozambique, so part of that gain is a cash transfer rather than a production effect [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is gross income from a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, and the authors note household overhead costs were also higher [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. The Indonesian result is second-hand, from a small sample, and compares against swidden cultivation rather than permanent cropland [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].

agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, IPCC assessments describe agroforestry limiting erosion and stabilising soils with perennial vegetation, and farmland with agroforestry is reported more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20–50% decrease in runoff, used here as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.conditionality: The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias, and Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3]. The IPCC statements are assessment-level, and several units are review statements without effect sizes [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5, ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_12, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control, with a weighted response ratio of 1.6 for soil moisture across 62 observations from 27 studies, and 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1 [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. Wetter soil under trees eases the crop's water stress. A cited statement adds that rainfall over agricultural land can shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.conditionality: The meta-analysis pools agroforestry practices without separating soil depth, so it cannot show whether trees and crops compete for deeper water; the Faidherbia parkland evidence that does show subsoil depletion sits in the regeneration-farmland row [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The effect on infiltration was greater than that on soil moisture [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect from a secondary citation, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Groundwater-recharge findings are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows.

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: Trees cut both ways in storms. A smallholder agroforestry review notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. A Latin American adaptation review gives planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The sides differ in what is exposed: the protective statement concerns sheltering and rebuilding on the farm, while the harmful example concerns trees falling on or damaging existing infrastructure [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. Placement relative to buildings and infrastructure is therefore the design point the evidence implies. Neither unit is a measured effect on livelihoods or crops: one is a typology example and the other a narrative review statement, and neither records a country or income group, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1].
