agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.mechanism: Trees and live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: trees were the main source of animal feed and milk production for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Zambian, US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems, and the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]; the understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size, and few units say how large the drought benefit is [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. No unit in this row measures the benefit in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.mechanism: A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row resting on two second-hand statements that point in opposite directions, so no clear effect can be drawn [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The silvopasture statement does not mention drought, and the shelterbelt finding concerns crop yield rather than an agro-pastoral outcome, applied here by default; neither transfers directly to LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral systems [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].

agroforestry__drought__all.mechanism: Most of the evidence finds that agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the finding splits by sub-practice and some measured results show no benefit or harm. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, and trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11].
agroforestry__drought__all.conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as clear benefits, the linear-boundary and cross-family cells as small benefits, and the shaded perennial-crop cell is conflicting. Few of the benefit units say how large the effect is, which also holds the class at moderate. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way: tree–maize competition for soil water in Kenya can lead to crop failure, and a Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2].

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In an induced-drought experiment in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping agroforestry system, crop losses occurred only in the monocropping system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row: all units come from Canada, Germany, the USA or temperate settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, which also notes N-fixation declined in both systems, the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions, and the US unit is a background statement that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. No unit says how large the effect is, and none measures it in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, a household survey and interviews conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought: households listed agroforestry as important for their livelihood during drought, in Burat households practising it mostly said droughts were less frequent while most households without it said the opposite, 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind, and farmers explained that deep roots let trees get water from deep down so they keep producing fruit when there is no rain [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also act as a fodder and cash reserve: in southern Zambia trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production during drought, in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet before the rains, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods while many farmers sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme stakeholders rated 14 of 22 cases as having a substantial or high effect on drought vulnerability, naming income from commercial agroforestry as one route that reduced vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression, and in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: Tree–crop competition can reverse the effect: a review cites Kenyan trials in which competition with Grevillea robusta for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and could lead to crop failure, an FAO review for Senegal finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought (some studies report higher yields near hedges in drier years, others harm to non-irrigated crops), and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. In Kinna, drought perceptions did not differ between households with and without agroforestry [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5], and the severe-drought evidence is a cited Honduran observation with no measured size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan resilience findings come from a single survey and are perception-based, the Zambian, Senegalese and competition findings are secondary citations in reviews, the Ethiopian rating credits a bundled programme rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In the Ghana cocoa experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline, and the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; both are among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline, and the cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific, entering because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.mechanism: Agroforestry raised soil moisture over controls (RR 1.6) in a sub-Saharan African meta-analysis, and a cited synthesis reports perennial trees added to cropland raise rainfall infiltration by 59% [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10]. Live fences supply fodder in the dry season when pasture is scarce, and shaded understorey crops can yield more than open systems under drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Ethiopia, income growth through commercial agroforestry is named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.conditionality: The quantified evidence is soil water, a component proxy for drought impact; the Ethiopian result is for a bundled land-management programme based on stakeholder responses, and the other units are reviews citing other studies [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. Only the Ethiopian unit names a country (low income); the rest are regional or pantropical reviews [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual farmers reported no total maize loss in the 1997 El Niño dry period, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Boundary plantings read as a small, unquantified benefit: a live-fence fodder role in drought, set against a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result sits outside the voting sub-practices, and that benefit reverses under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: Both units point to a benefit, but neither says how large it is, and neither measures a severe or extreme drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. This is a high-income temperate scope row (Canada, Germany) outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, and the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: The evidence for rainfed cropping points both ways. A review cites Kenyan trials in which maize grown with Grevillea robusta competed with the trees for limited soil water, which delayed maize flowering and development and could lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Against this, the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme income growth through commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: An FAO review for Senegal reports no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought: some studies find higher yields near hedges in drier years, while others judge the hedges could harm non-irrigated crops; and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. Whether trees help or hurt the crop in drought turns on how strongly they compete for limited soil water [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Much of the pool is second-hand: the competition result and both review findings are secondary citations, the Ethiopian rating belongs to a bundled programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation and agroforestry) rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the source of the Nigerian model notes its weak fit may understate impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock settings the evidence points the same way, though few units say how large the effect is, so the class is a slight reduction in drought impact. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Brazilian semi-arid, agroforestry biomass productivity varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, which the source attributes mainly to water availability, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species carry livestock through dry periods with high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.conditionality: The Kenyan household units are a single study of survey and farmer-interview evidence, and the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. No unit measures the effect in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: On pastoral land the benefit runs through fodder and herd condition. Live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species are used to feed livestock in the dry season and supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In Colombia, a review citing Altieri and Nicholls 2013 reports that forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011) [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The evidence base is thin and mostly second-hand: the silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume, the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Only the Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland systems; the live-fence review, the understorey statement and the Kenyan FMNR rating are applied here by default [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, when tree shade could decrease understorey yields [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Colombian sources are upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The units point in opposite directions and neither measures drought losses in a pastoral system: the shelterbelt result is a temperate cropping finding applied to pastoral rangeland by default, and the Costa Rican result is dry-season liveweight gain [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Both are earlier findings cited second-hand, from high-income or temperate settings outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: Against those benefits, a model-based assessment cited in a tropical agroforestry review (Onyekuru and Marchant) found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues in Nigeria under a simulated climate 1◦C warmer with 7% less annual rainfall; it enters as an income proxy and is the no-benefit result that discounts the class [ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran observation repeats Welchez and Cherrett, cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. None of the units records a pastoral or rangeland farming system: the Honduran unit concerns crops and the others name no system, so they are applied to rangeland by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. All units are from lower-middle-income countries (Honduras, Kenya, Nigeria), inside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: All units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. The El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm, and the deep-root forage unit refers to the dry season without a size [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. The evidence comes from upper-middle-income Latin America, outside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.mechanism: Under drought, trees in tree-crop systems have been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin) and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]; and a review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. General agroforestry reports point the same way: live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms (Blaser et al.), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; the field study by Abdulai et al. in Ghana measured this directly: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 against 170 in full sun (grams per square centimetre per day), sap flux recovered to 163 in full sun but only 37 under A. toxicaria, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade may not prevent the yield decline under drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.conditionality: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses are attributed to that competition, measured in the Ghanaian shade-tree study (Abdulai et al.) as lower soil water under the shade trees than in full sun, while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia), a shade-management setting (canopy openness) or a drought year in which shade relieved the understorey [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A second separator is what is measured: the Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment found the overall better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought, so a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Shade-tree species is a third: in the Abdulai study every cocoa plant under Albizia ferruginea died against 77% under Antiaris toxicaria [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions for drought-exposed tree-crop systems. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the throughfall-exclusion experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Many units on both sides are second-hand readings in reviews [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; the Abdulai shade-tree study, measured on a single farm, is the field anchor of the harm side [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; the live-fence, FMNR and understorey units record none and are applied here by default, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The field units are from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.mechanism: Studies disagree on what trees do to tree crops in drought in low- and lower-middle-income settings. On the benefit side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade trees strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1], and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the harm side, a field study in Ghana found that during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to stronger competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.conditionality: Several units find no effect either way. In a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment on cocoa, the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it; the shade there came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The same Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. What separates gains from losses is shade management and how severe the shock is: the Ethiopian gain appears at high canopy openness, while the Ghana deaths came under dense shade trees in an extreme drought [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The harm finding is a direct measurement while the benefit units are a yield model and a compiler rating, which is why the harm side carries real weight despite resting on a single study [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Only the cocoa and coffee units are measured in tree-crop systems; they are crop-specific and enter under the shaded perennial-crop scope ruling, while the Kenyan FMNR rating is applied to tree-crop systems by default [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].

agroforestry__drought_hazard.mechanism: Trees on farms slightly reduce the damage drought does to farm households. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, that trees were the most important source of animal food and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought (Chibinga et al. 2012), that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce, and that agroforestry biomass production varied less over 4 years than conventional systems in semi-arid Brazil, attributed mainly to water availability (Martins et al. 2013) [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__drought_hazard.conditionality: Effects are not uniform, and for some adopters the trees made drought losses worse. During the extreme drought of 2015/16 in Ghana, a field study found that all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Elsewhere, a review says tree shade could decrease understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreaks in drought, some studies finding higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. In Kenya the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit states only that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Few units give a size, so the class is slight. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household and fodder evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya and low-income Zambia, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__establishment_cost.mechanism: The programme reports adoption costs of $66 per household and $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana, and $201 per household and $1,387 per hectare for tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_3, ev_project_cost_crs23_4].
agroforestry__establishment_cost.conditionality: These are programme expenditures per adopting household or per adopted hectare, two denominators that cannot be pooled, from two arms of one programme (Ghana lower-middle, Rwanda low income) [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_3, ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. The quote does not identify them as establishment costs specifically, and they are levels rather than costs relative to a control [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_2, ev_project_cost_crs23_3, ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__fire__agro_pastoral.mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. A land-use overlay of burnt areas across six European Mediterranean countries found that, corrected for the extent of each land use, agroforestry occupied 12% of the area but was associated with only 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40%; agroforestry's share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Before that correction, the average share of fire incidents was lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
agroforestry__fire__agro_pastoral.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state rather than the farming-system counterfactual this cell asks about. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8], and the Mediterranean overlay compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland, not with the cropland or open pasture a project would convert [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6], and in the Mediterranean data grassland, not agroforestry, had the lowest unadjusted share of fires [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. The Mediterranean result that does favour agroforestry is the one against shrubland; against forest and grassland the difference was not significant [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Both studies come from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; in the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of agroforestry against the treeless farmland or pasture it replaces, ideally in an LIC/LMIC system. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is carried but cannot set the class either: it is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. It concerns natural regeneration rather than silvopasture, but its direction agrees with the comparator argument above: added tree cover adds fuel, and the compiler recommends fire breaks for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].

agroforestry__fire__agro_pastoral__incom.mechanism: In European Mediterranean countries, once fire counts are corrected for the extent of each land use, agroforestry areas (grazed dehesa and montado-type wood-pasture) occupied 12% of the area but were associated with only 6% of fires, while shrublands occupied 16% and carried 40%; the agroforestry share was not statistically different from forest or grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Under Regreening Africa the share of respondents consuming at least five of the ten food items rose from 16 to 21, a 31 percent increase, and households that intensified their use of tree products saw significant gains in dietary diversity [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. In the Nepal mid-hills the share of food-sufficient households rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry project, and in Nyando, Kenya, agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies in hunger periods, some relying on tree fruit when floods washed their crops away [ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. In Talensi, Ghana, the share of households with one or more hungry months fell from 68.2% to 41% between the 2017 baseline and the 2020 endline [ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. In the East Usambara Mountains of Tanzania, improved agroforestry was securing enough food throughout the year for 40% of households against 18% of households using traditional practices [ev_food_security_reyes05_1].
agroforestry__food_insecurity.conditionality: The benefit is not universal. In Rwanda more trees went with higher food security in Congo Nile but with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands, a measured harm for farmers there [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. In Maradi, Niger, FMNR did not appear to reduce the months of perceived food shortage, a Kenyan improved-fallow study found no significant results on nutritional measurements, and the Regreening Africa FIES score showed no substantial change, moving from 4.9 to 4.8 [ev_food_security_haglund11_1, ev_food_security_castle21s_2, ev_food_security_rgaf23_9]. The Campbell systematic review found the impact on nutrition and food security beneficial or neutral, never harmful, across the studies it covered [ev_food_security_castle21s_4]. The Tanzanian contrast is not an experiment and is not trees alone: the improved farms bundle multipurpose trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, and they are larger, keep more dairy cattle and have more off-farm income than the traditional farms they are compared with [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan review gives no pooled estimate for food security, and it notes that outcomes vary with agroforestry type, complementary practices and context [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. Several gains come from before-and-after project surveys with no control group: the Nepal result belongs to a bundled project that added market linkage, training, subsidies and organic fertiliser to the trees, and the Talensi and Regreening Africa figures are project endlines [ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_food_security_rgaf23_8]. The Malawi, Zambia and Kenya effect sizes are earlier studies cited in that review, and the IPCC unit is an assessment statement rather than a measured effect [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_castle21s_3, ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7]. Regeneration-based practices alone show only a slight effect; the moderate class rests on the cross-practice evidence.

agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock systems, trees give households food and saleable products that carry them through hunger periods. In the Nepal mid-hills the share of food-sufficient households rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry project, a change the authors report as highly significant [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Tanzania's East Usambara Mountains, improved agroforestry secured enough food throughout the year for 40% of households against 18% of households using traditional practices, even though the latter grew mainly food crops [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Nyando, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and some farmers had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when floods put other crops underwater [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. In Rwanda, tree density was associated with higher food security in some agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1].
agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.conditionality: The effect depends on site: in Rwanda's Buberuka Highlands more trees went with lower food security, a measured harm, while in Congo Nile the association ran the other way [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The sizes come from comparisons without a randomised control: the Nepal figure is a before-and-after survey of project households in a project that bundled the trees with market linkage, training, subsidies and organic fertiliser, and the Tanzanian improved systems bundle multipurpose trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, so neither gain belongs to the trees alone [ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. The Kenyan flood-fruit finding is farmer-reported [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The evidence comes from Kenya, Nepal, Rwanda and Tanzania.

agroforestry__frost__agro_pastoral.mechanism: At night the tree canopy keeps under-storey temperatures higher, protecting crops from frost damage, especially in winter [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3]. Brazilian sources report that trees reduce wind, raise minimum temperatures and reduce night-time radiative losses, minimising frost damage, and that a closed canopy in a denser planting line is expected to have lowered night-time radiation losses and plant damage [ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5].
agroforestry__frost__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The cell rests on microclimate evidence (night-time canopy temperature and radiation), a component of frost impact, rather than measured frost losses on farms [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5]. Brazilian units (upper-middle income) and a review statement has no recorded country or income group; none is from an LIC/LMIC setting, and the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3]. All three are reviews or authors citing earlier work, and none records a farming system, so the evidence is applied to each farming system by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5].
