agroforestry__gender_inequity.mechanism: A gender review finds agroforestry can offer substantial benefits to women, but their participation is low in enterprises considered men's domain such as timber and in the area and number of trees they commit [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1]. It reports, second-hand, that management labour often falls on women (in 89% of Embu households using calliandra fodder, females managed it) [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2], that 32% of males and 23% of females planted improved fallows in four Zambian villages [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3], and that in farmer-managed trials women had somewhat higher Sesbania survival than men [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4].
agroforestry__gender_inequity.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: every unit comes from a single narrative review of sub-Saharan African studies, read second-hand, with no measured finding of its own [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.mechanism: In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside, and access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Senegal Ferlo and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems; the rest are general reviews applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. All units report cooling or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact, and all are reviews or assessments citing earlier studies, the Ferlo temperatures repeating Akpo et al. [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. Reviews and syntheses report the same cooling more generally: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C and soil temperature by 6–10°C, agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise coffee yields, and shade trees produce microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air temperature under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside, and access to the cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. In cocoa and coffee, a pantropical synthesis found mean temperature lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures buffered in cocoa agroforestry against monocultures, a review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, and measurements in Costa Rican coffee found shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all.conditionality: Cooling under trees is consistent across the units, but most measure temperature or animal comfort rather than a heat-stress loss to crops, herds or income, and none measures the effect in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, so the class is a slight reduction. Against the cooling, windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Nearly all units are reviews citing earlier studies. The yield and milk-production units apply to hot conditions only, and the German alley-cropping unit is high-income temperate evidence [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The IPCC chapter that says shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee adds in the same sentence that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; they report temperature rather than heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: On hot summer days, a poplar alley-cropping system in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than a sole wheat system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture, and cited studies found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than for cows in full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C against full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units come from Germany or Costa Rica, recorded as high income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; all but the coffee measurement are earlier studies cited in reviews [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. The coffee unit is crop-specific and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. They report air temperature or milk yield rather than measured heat-stress losses, live fences gave the smallest cooling of the arrangements compared, and the milk gain is not separated from other effects of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: In Ethiopia, Faidherbia albida trees cut the radiation reaching the wheat canopy and made the wheat 6°C cooler than open wheat [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5]. In the Ferlo, Senegal, air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged less widely than outside the canopy, and in Kenya shade trees are described as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations and can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal pull the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots with impacts that depend on the crop and its growth stage, so the evidence pools opposite signs [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. All four units are from LIC/LMIC countries (Ethiopia, Kenya, Senegal), but all are reported second-hand from earlier studies and rest on temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In Cuba, live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units are reviews citing earlier studies, and they report animal comfort rather than measured production losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.mechanism: Reviews report that tree shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Shade from live fences is reported to reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.conditionality: No unit records irrigated cropping; the evidence is applied here by default, and the cattle-shade units concern livestock rather than irrigated crops [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The only recorded country is Cuba (upper-middle income); the other five units have no country or income group, so the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies and rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The Ethiopian, German, Indian, Senegalese and Chinese units come from rainfed cropping, and the German unit is high-income temperate evidence; the yield gain applies to hot conditions only [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies and report cooling, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.mechanism: For mixed systems with cattle, a Brazilian comparison found 20 to 100% reductions in areas at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals under agroforestry compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. For crops, shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, and in Kenya shade trees are described as buffering temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.conditionality: The cell rests on proxy/component evidence (animal thermal comfort and air temperature) rather than direct measurement of heat-stress losses, which is why its class is capped [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1]. Only the Brazilian and Kenyan units are recorded as mixed crop-livestock; the others carry no or a different farming system and are applied by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Contexts are Kenya (lower-middle income), Brazil (upper-middle) and further units with no context, all reported second-hand, so the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it (Ocampo et al. 2012) [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain (Abreu 2002) [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In Nicaragua, Betancourt et al. 2003 found milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun (Souza et al. 2000) [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. General reviews report the same cooling: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects in silvopasture as well as crop systems, and tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: Every unit reports a benefit, but none measures it in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, and the transfer to LIC/LMIC rangelands is not direct: almost all the weight sits in upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and unlocated reviews, with Nicaragua the only lower-middle-income site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures are associations with shade rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: The Colombian unit is a review citing an earlier study (Ocampo et al.) that reports animal comfort without a size, and the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself, though its comparison of woody-cover levels is cited from an earlier study [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Latin America, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.mechanism: Shade over tree crops lowers the temperature the crop experiences. Reviews report that over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, that tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C (Liu et al. 2019), that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress (Arenas-Corraliza et al. 2018; Sida et al. 2018), and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee (Rahn et al. 2014, 2018) [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A coffee review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress (Lin et al. 2008; Meylan et al. 2017), and the IPCC notes, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.conditionality: Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not say how much that cuts crop or income losses, so the class is slight: all units rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact, and none measures the effect in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme. The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees for coffee adds that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; they are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, while the general review statements are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies. The cocoa meta-analysis is weighted towards Ghana (lower-middle income), the Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high income, and several units have no country or income group, so the transfer to the LIC/LMIC target is adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Tree shade lowers temperatures where crops and animals sit: poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, Faidherbia albida canopies lowered midday air temperature over Ethiopian wheat by up to 6°C against the open field, and reviews report shade buffering temperature effects by 2–4°C and lowering ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Shade from live fences and silvopastoral models reduces cattle heat stress, and a Brazilian comparison found 20 to 100% reductions in areas at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Associated trees buffer air and soil temperature, reduce wind and raise humidity under the canopy, and tree cover protects crops against extreme microclimate fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. A systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on biophysical variables mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air, black globe and soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]; an older cattle review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade, combining protection from sunlight with cooling as moisture evaporates from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, and under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall in tropical agroforestry systems temperature is about 2°C lower than at a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found mean temperature lower and daily extremes buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], a coffee review reports, second-hand, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. In a Ghanaian cocoa field, the role of shade trees in moderating microclimate was confirmed especially in the dry and extremely dry periods, when daily mean maximum air temperatures were significantly higher, reaching up to 44°C, in the comparison with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: The cooling is consistent, but the class is slight because the cell rests on proxy/component evidence (air and canopy temperature, microclimate, animal thermal comfort) rather than direct measurement of heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Windbreak hedges in Senegal point the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots, so opposite signs are pooled [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Not every index shows the cooling: in the dairy review, of the 12 studies with animals, seven used only the temperature humidity index, and four of the seven found no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]; the review attributes this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main route by which trees cut heat load. Cooling is also not the same as protection: in the Ghanaian cocoa study, the study notes record that its authors concluded the cooling did not protect the cocoa because competition with the shade trees for soil water overrode it [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. Evidence spans Ethiopia (low income), Kenya and Senegal (lower-middle), Brazil, China, Colombia, Cuba and Mexico (upper-middle) and Germany and Costa Rica (high), plus reviews with no recorded context, most of them reported second-hand, though the Ethiopian canopy temperature was measured directly on farm [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, the dairy systematic review is mostly upper-middle-income Brazil, the Kelly et al. statement reaches this row second-hand from high-income Australian and US cattle work [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1], while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific to shaded perennial systems, and some carry their source's own caveat: IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate rising temperatures for arabica coffee but that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2], and the coffee review notes that in parts of East Africa excessive shade with heavy rain raised fungal infection risk [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In Senegal's Ferlo, minimum and maximum air temperatures under the canopy of Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C, against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Both units are earlier studies cited in reviews and report air temperature under tree canopies, a component of heat-stress impact rather than a measured heat-stress outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In the Ferlo the canopy narrowed the range in both directions, with a higher minimum as well as a lower maximum under the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: In rainfed cropping, trees and shelterbelts cool the crop. Under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C against the open field, peaking at 29oC under the canopy versus 36oC outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland found shelterbelts reduced summer air temperature by 4.01% against unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1], and a review reports, second-hand, that poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: an FAO review in Senegal states, second-hand, that windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage, so shelter designs that cut wind may warm rather than cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The units measure air temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not heat-stress yield losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. They span low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal, upper-middle-income China and high-income Germany [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: In Brazil, eucalyptus–brachiaria agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture, and in semi-arid Kenya shade trees are cited as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations, which in turn can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Both units are cited statements from a review or a study's introduction rather than the sources' own measurements, and they report animal thermal comfort and microclimate, components of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. The Brazilian unit is upper-middle income and the Kenyan unit lower-middle income [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopastoral systems for dairy cows, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.mechanism: Linear tree plantings have been found both to raise and to lower yields. Gains come from shelter: windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% by protecting plants from winter desiccation, protected plots in the Senegal River valley showed a 23 per cent total yield increase in the off-season, crop yield was 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland in a Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis, and live fences can improve soil fertility and crop yields provided tree roots are deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows found they raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68), counted here as a component of the production gap; hedgerow litter and the capture of nutrient-laden sediment from runoff supply it [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Losses come from competition and shade: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], cereal yields next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years of a field study [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1], excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14], and in the West African Sahel live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Hedgerow intercropping in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis gave a response ratio of 0.9, an interval touching no effect [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. A global quantitative review of paddocks with windbreaks found yield reduced by 8.3% on average against paddocks with no windbreaks, excluding the land occupied by the trees, with more decreases (n = 171) than increases (n = 83): crop yield −9.2% and crop biomass −9.3%, while pasture showed a small average increase of +3.1% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. In the same Saskatchewan study the sheltered zone beyond the competition strip gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but against the mid-field yield the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, while doubting that baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The global review's distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.conditionality: The evidence itself names most of what separates gains from losses. Season: in the Saskatchewan study the sheltered-zone gain appeared in 1989 and 1990 but was absent in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, which the authors attribute to high actual evapotranspiration by the crops [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the Saskatchewan shelterbelt units are measured but high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. The hedgerow soil-nitrogen pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil concentration, not yield, so it shows a pathway to higher output rather than the output itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.mechanism: Boundary and line plantings earn money from the tree products. A windbreak hedge in irrigated rice in the Senegal River valley had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent counting its woody products [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields of Haryana, India, a biodrainage review reports from Ram et al. (2011) that eucalyptus strip plantations on farm boundaries, which need only an initial investment, gave a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 over the first rotation through fodder, wood or fibre harvested [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. Neotropical farmers perceive live fences as a source of additional income, for example from timber sales [ev_household_income_moran18_7].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.conditionality: All the units are second-hand: the returns are financial indicators and the income claim a farmer perception, each used as a proxy for poverty, and none measures household poverty or how the gain is shared [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3, ev_household_income_moran18_7]. The strength is therefore not quantified. Both financial results come from irrigated systems (rice in Senegal, wheat inter-spaces in canal-irrigated Haryana), in lower-middle-income countries within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]; in the Haryana case the trees were planted to drain waterlogged land, so the return comes with that purpose [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.mechanism: Live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used in Colombia, Mexico and Nigeria to prevent erosion and retain soil moisture, live fences in India reduce erosion by lowering runoff velocity, and Kenyan farmers report that planting trees in a line prevents soil being swept away by water [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. A global review of plot and field studies found linear tree plantings (windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows) cut soil loss by 55% on average against land without them, the lowest of the agroforestry systems compared though the differences among systems were not significant [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.conditionality: Only the review figure states a size, which is why the class stops at moderate; the other units are cited review statements, a farmer quote and a soil-marker comparison without erosion rates [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The 55% is an average of compiled study reductions across temperate and tropical sites, not a weighted meta-analytic effect, and it is not specific to low-income settings [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.mechanism: Windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows on farmland hold soil and nutrients on the field through surface cover and fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies found linear tree plantings decreased the average nutrient loss from leaching and runoff by 16% and 33% respectively, against land without them [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.conditionality: Confidence is very low: the row rests on a single review with few case studies for linear plantings, the percentages are averages of compiled study results rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, and no country or income group is given [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The ranges across studies are wide and include no change: phosphorus losses fell by 0–50%, and the nitrogen range runs from an increase to a large decrease [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The review also reports that linear plantings reduced nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium losses less than the other agroforestry systems it covered. The unit measures nutrient loss leaving the field, which is the pathway to water quality downstream, not stream or groundwater quality itself.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.mechanism: One study links field shelterbelts to more water stress, through less soil water next to the trees. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The engine reads a slight, unquantified increase in water stress; the counterfactual is soil further into the same field, not an unsheltered field.
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.conditionality: This rests on one source. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Missing: measured soil water or crop water stress beside windbreaks, live fences or hedgerows in low- or lower-middle-income settings, and any study that compares sheltered with unsheltered fields.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.mechanism: Deep-rooted, fast-growing boundary trees can drain waterlogged fields by transpiring excess soil water (biodrainage). A review of biodrainage cites a study by Ram et al. (2011) in canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, Haryana, India: parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis along farm boundaries, spaced at 66 m at a density of 300 plants per hectare, lowered the groundwater table beneath the strips by 85 cm compared with adjacent unvegetated fields in 3 years, with wheat grown between the strips [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.conditionality: No class is set because the row rests on one second-hand reading of one Indian study. What is missing is a second independent source or a direct measurement, ideally one that reports crop yield or farm income on the drained land rather than water-table depth alone; the water-table fall is measured under the strips, and how far it extends into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].

The study was in canal-irrigated fields, so it matches this farming system directly.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind speed over a zone that typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large landscapes need multiple barriers to control wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. Live fences in India serve as windbreaks and raise soil moisture retention through litter build-up [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: Both units are reviews citing earlier studies and concern wind erosion and sheltering, not cyclone damage [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. Only the Indian unit names a country (lower-middle income) [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks, hedges and live fences slow the wind: the zone of reduced wind speed typically extends 10 to 20 times tree height downwind (Tibke 1988), hedges have a major impact on wind and protect sandy, poorly covered soils from wind erosion in Senegal, and live fences serve as windbreaks in India [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found wind speed 35.80% lower in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: Every unit reports less wind, but the units describe windbreak function in general rather than measured storm or cyclone losses to crops or income, and none measures the effect in a storm the authors call severe or extreme, so the evidence does not say whether the protection holds at cyclone strength. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies; the Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis is the one measured synthesis, and it measures everyday wind speed in upper-middle-income China [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The Senegal and India units are from lower-middle-income countries inside the LIC/LMIC target, and the downwind-extent unit names no location [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. The Senegal hedge and Chinese shelterbelt units come from rainfed cropping; the others are applied to all farming systems by default.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.conditionality: The strong class rests on a single trial and a single taxon: earthworm diversity is a soil-biodiversity indicator, not a measure of wider farm or landscape biodiversity, and statistical significance of the difference is not reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. The system was fertilised and given need-based irrigation at tree establishment, so the result applies to managed alley systems on degraded lateritic soils in lower-middle-income settings; further studies, on other taxa, are needed before this reads as a general effect.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.mechanism: Trees planted into cropland add carbon to the soil through leaf litter, prunings and roots, raising soil carbon storage above that of the crop grown alone. In a ten-year trial on degraded red and lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon under a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system reached 0.59% against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from an initial 0.30% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, consistent with earlier syntheses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. In southern Malawi, Tephrosia vogelii relay-planted under maize keeps growing into the dry season and returns nitrogen-rich leafy residues; at Songani soil C under this intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.conditionality: The direction is consistent, but not every site shows a clear gain. The Malawi difference was a trend that was not significant (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1], and at Sadore, Niger, the block with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held from 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without after four years of millet and cowpea, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. The Niger trial compares two blocks with tree presence neither randomised nor replicated, so block differences are mixed into the contrast [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Soil carbon is a component of carbon removal, measured here as a stock or concentration, not as a removal rate, and tree biomass storage is not counted in this row [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. The strongest gain comes from a long-running research-station trial on degraded soil, where the starting carbon was low [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. The field evidence is from low-income Malawi and Niger and lower-middle-income India, all rainfed cropping; the meta-analysis is global [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Rwanda, where the arm was tree-planting agroforestry, cost $201 per household [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one low-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. The same quote attributes Rwanda's higher per-household cost than Ghana's FMNR to tree-planting agroforestry where average land size per household is much more limited [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Rwanda, where the arm was tree-planting agroforestry, cost $1,387 per hectare [ev_project_cost_crs23_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per hectare where at least one practice was adopted, from one low-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. The same quote notes the much more limited average land size per household in Rwanda and gives $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana [ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: Planted tree-crop systems in annual cropping add labour, and costs rise with it. In Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping in a maize/groundnut intercrop raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%), and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In Nigeria, maize plots mulched with tree prunings required higher labour input than the fertilizer and untreated controls, 96% of it for collecting and managing mulch and only 4% for weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: The cost rise comes from the work of cutting, carrying and spreading prunings, so the design and harvest regime of the hedgerows set the bill [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and they decreased from the first to the third year, so the 34% is an average that is heavier early on [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In the Nigerian trial the trees were grown on a separate plot and the prunings carried in, a biomass-transfer design rather than trees in the field itself [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both are on-station or researcher-run trials in lower-middle-income West and Central Africa; the size rests on the Cameroon figure alone, and neither unit is a cost saving.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: The only unit names income growth through commercial agroforestry as one option that reduced vulnerability to climate shocks (drought) in some Ethiopian communities; it gives no biophysical mechanism [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: The rated effect belongs to a bundled sustainable-land-management programme assessed through stakeholder responses, not to agroforestry alone, and it does not describe a planted silvoarable design [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. The evidence is from Ethiopia (low income), within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Sahel, a study cited in a Brazilian review (Bogie et al. 2018) found millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, reported in the IPCC chapter from Nasielski et al. 2015, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: Tree–crop competition can reverse the effect: in Kenyan maize with Grevillea robusta, a study cited in a review (Lott et al. 2009) found that competition for limited soil water delays maize flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. The Kenyan units are a single household study of survey and farmer-interview evidence; the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The Canadian experiment is high-income temperate evidence [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The German alley-cropping soil-water result is high-income temperate evidence, a component measure, and not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. None of the units measures the effect under a drought the authors call severe or extreme, so the class says nothing about the worst droughts.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: The only unit names income growth through commercial agroforestry as one option that reduced vulnerability to climate shocks (drought) in some Ethiopian communities; it gives no biophysical mechanism [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: The rated effect belongs to a bundled sustainable-land-management programme assessed through stakeholder responses, not to agroforestry alone, and it does not describe a planted silvoarable design [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. The evidence is from Ethiopia (low income), within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: Woody plants in a crop field under drought have been found both to protect the crop and to compete with it for water. On the protective side, in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, in a study set up to test whether hydraulic redistribution by the shrub benefits the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]; in an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]; and in a German alley-cropping system in a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though not significantly at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. On the competing side, in Kenyan maize with Grevillea robusta, competition for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and development and can lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the woody species and the crop draw on the same limited soil water: the loss is attributed to that competition in a maize and Grevillea system [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10], whereas the largest gain is with a shrub studied for its redistribution of water to the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. The choice of tree and crop combination is therefore the design question for drought-exposed rainfed cropping. Both sides carry weaknesses. A systematic review reports yield gains for soil-fertility replenishment practices where soil fertility is severely depleted, and in Ethiopia land productivity improved where nitrogen-fixing trees were incorporated into the farming system [ev_t6_yield_soilfert_castle21_2, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. A meta-analysis of woody legumes in maize across West, East and southern Africa found yield increases over unfertilized maize of 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes, and response ratios of 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2]. In Cameroon's humid forest zone, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots increased from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control plot decreased, and groundnut pod yield was also higher in the alleys [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1]. In the Sahel of Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased millet yields by 41 % in the control without fertilizer and by 10 % with farmyard manure, and millet yields in the millet/cowpea intercrop by 8 and 11 % in the same treatments [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; crop incomes rose 5 to 14 % without counting the tree's fruit, and 2 to 3 times with it [ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. Across 333 paddock years in a global quantitative review, alleys reduced yield by 17.63% on average and only 69 responses showed increases; paddocks with spacings between alleys under 10 tree heights were predicted to lose yield, with a reduction of more than 25% under 2.5 tree heights, while at 15 tree heights the predicted paddock yield increase was 13% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8].

What separates them, as far as the evidence says, is the comparison and the inputs. The large gains are measured against unfertilized maize on depleted African soils, with leguminous trees supplying nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3, ev_t6_yield_soilfert_castle21_2]; once mineral fertiliser is applied, the tree benefit can vanish or reverse.
