Tree age and spacing matter: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and alfalfa 51.83% less than sole crops [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; in a global review, alleys reduced paddock yield by 17.63% on average, narrow spacings lose yield and the largest spacings gain [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. Other losses: a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme lowered crop value, water competition with Grevillea robusta delayed Kenyan maize, intercropped wheat, maize and soybean yielded less than monocultures in China, Indonesia and Brazil, and Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2]; some stability models at Msekera ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. Some results sit at no effect: improved fallows were not significant in a Kenyan production-function estimate, a Tephrosia relay intercrop in southern Malawi gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, and in Niger the soil with Ziziphus held 10 to 15 % more nitrogen than the soil without, a difference that was not significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6, ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Study caveats: the Niger trial placed its trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and its contrasts carry block effects [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1]; the Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. The magnitude range runs from a single-digit wheat gain to a more-than-900% crop biomass gain under water stress in a Sahelian shrub intercrop, so it does not describe a typical effect [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. The global alley review gives no country or income-group breakdown, and its alley group includes pasture alleys and hedges [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6]; the Xinjiang losses come from an irrigated upper-middle-income system with trees in their first years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. For a project, the fertiliser regime, the crop grown in the alleys and the tree spacing are the design questions.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for 4 years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. In Ethiopia, market-oriented agroforestry with Acacia decurrens is credited with income, employment and reduced poverty in supported microwatersheds [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. On-station and on-farm trials that cost both systems show trees with crops earning more than either alone: in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave a net benefit of US$4148 per hectare against US$2386 for the traditional treeless maize/groundnut intercrop [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]; in North Kordofan, Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal gum plantation out-earned the same crops grown alone: sorghum gave a net revenue of 558 SDG per hectare against 501 SDG as a sole crop, sesame 300 against 205, and roselle 518 against 389 [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]; and in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system gave net returns 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a 10-year cycle, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. In southwestern Nigeria, a sweet orange orchard intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus had a net present value of N 154300 and one intercropped with cassava and maize N 105900, against N -37900 for the monocropped orchard, which yielded no revenue in its first years while the intercropped plots earned throughout [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. Trees can also compensate for crop losses: a review of 74 articles found the share of studies reporting harm fell from 36% for yield to 16% for overall livelihood effects, and where trees raised food yield the livelihood effect was positive in 86% of studies [ev_household_income_reed17_1, ev_household_income_reed17_2, ev_household_income_reed17_3]. In Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot intercrops gave a higher average cash flow than sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.conditionality: The gains depend on land, labour and input costs, and some adopters lose. In south-western Nigeria, mulching maize with leaves cut and carried from a multipurpose-tree plot gave higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer only when the land under the trees was not valued; where land is scarce the technology is unprofitable in both the short and long term [ev_economic_return_korm99_5, ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In West Bengal the benefit–cost ratio of sole pigeon pea was higher than that of pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, so the higher net return came with higher costs [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. Several effects did not reach significance or reversed: Zambian improved fallows raised maize income but not total crop income, Kenyan improved fallows changed liquid assets but not significantly, and crop–fruit tree intercropping in China (Dai et al., 2017) lowered gross income [ev_household_income_castle21s_4, ev_household_income_castle21s_5, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; in western Kenya small farm sizes limited the impact of improved fallows on poverty even though they were attractive to the poor [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are net returns or net present values from research-managed trials, components of household income rather than measured poverty change [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Nigerian orchard compares trees with crops against trees alone, so it shows the value of the crops in the alleys rather than of adding trees to a field [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Ethiopian unit is an evaluation lesson rather than a measured effect [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. The Zambian figures are an earlier study cited in an ICRAF working paper and compare losses on crop failure rather than incomes [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.mechanism: Trees combined with crops, as alley cropping, contour hedgerow intercropping or tree intercropping, protect the soil surface with living plants, litter and mulch and bind it with extended fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies against sole crops found silvoarable agroforestry cut soil loss by 66% on average and water loss by 43% [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.conditionality: Confidence is very low because the row rests on a single review: the percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and the review gives no country or income-group breakdown, so the fit to LIC/LMIC settings is unknown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. The soil-loss reduction did not differ significantly among the agroforestry systems the review compared, while silvoarable systems cut water loss less than silvopastoral systems (73%) [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. Runoff reduction is counted here as a component of erosion risk. How much soil is saved on a given field will depend on slope, rainfall and how the hedgerows or tree rows are laid out, which the review does not resolve.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: The direction comes mainly from a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, now joined by a Ziziphus trial in the Sahel. Water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99, and 2.41 against 0.87 for gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea against maize + pigeonpea in 1999/00 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. Available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration from improved soil structure and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 17 % in the control and by 11 % with manure on millet and SSP1 on cowpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year adds that soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The same Malawi trial also records harm: the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Other measurements found no difference: a generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The direction leans on water use efficiency figures. In Malawi these are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]. Gliricidia biomass lifts the tree-system values, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated; these units count for water stress only and are held out of the production gap because they do not measure crop yield. Timing and depth set the limits: the trees deplete dry-season and subsoil water, so crops may start the season with less, while recharge-season water favours the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. The result holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the crop season and left unpruned after harvest; unpruned or denser tree rows are not covered [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5]. The evidence comes from research-station trials in southern Malawi and in Niger. The Niger trial set its trees in a single block and its tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised or replicated across blocks and the contrast carries block effects; its gains are reported for the unfertilised, manure and SSP1 treatments [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. Both are low-income settings within the LIC/LMIC target. The German trial counts little: a temperate high-income site whose differences were not significant at all positions, measuring surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth, as a review reports from Dhillon et al. (2010) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: the only evidence is a single Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review, with no size stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look. The study system is irrigated cropping, applied here to all farming systems by default [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth, as a review reports from Dhillon et al. (2010) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: the only evidence is a single Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review, with no size stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__production_gap.mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems now lean to a gain, but still record tree–crop competition losses next to the fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt study is measured, but it is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; its net loss is measured against the mid-field yield rather than an unsheltered field, a baseline the authors themselves question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. At Sadore the Ziziphus gain depended on the fertiliser: millet yield fell by 13 % under the trees with NPK, intercropped millet fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK and manure, and cowpea fell by 15 % in the unfertilised control, probably from tree shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; soil N there did not differ significantly with and without the trees, and tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated across the two blocks [ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Young fruit trees compete hard: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated semi-arid Xinjiang, China (upper-middle income), soybean yield fell by 46.03% and alfalfa by 51.83% against sole crops, partly because the intercrop had a smaller cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Sileshi maize meta-analysis compares against unfertilised maize, not farmer practice with fertiliser, and its authors note signs of publication bias [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1]; the hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Parkland trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, crucial in the dry season and during drought, and in Senegal access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected by tree cover [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Cereals lose out: grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, so the net effect depends on which crops dominate [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies from the Sahel and Senegal, and the fodder and livestock gains are stated without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light. Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The class rests on a single Chinese experiment with young trees, so confidence is low and the size may not hold as the trees mature or in other designs [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Part of the Chinese loss reflects the smaller cropped area and the lower seeding rate and irrigation given to the intercropped soybean, and yields are per unit of total plot area, so the tree rows count against the crop [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. The Senegal result runs the other way over the whole protected plot, which separates the two: hedges bordering a plot lose crop near the hedge but can raise the plot total, while trees planted through the plot at close spacing take crop area and water directly [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading in grey literature with no comparator stated beyond the unprotected plots. China is upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target; Senegal is lower-middle income, within it [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In the Brazilian semi-arid, tree leaves added nitrogen in a cactus pear and buffel grass association, with potential to cut fertiliser cost, and a silvopastoral system gave higher mean bodyweight gain per animal than the monoculture [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The Kenyan productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and soil nitrogen is a component rather than a yield measure [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. The Brazilian units are cited secondary results from an upper-middle-income country, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, while the Kenyan unit is lower-middle income [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In rangeland and pasture systems trees raise livestock output through forage, shade and higher stocking. In the Senegalese Ferlo, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies was 2 to 5 times that of treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diets late in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In Latin American silvopasture, tree shade is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]; milk was 32.1% higher in intensive silvopasture than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Stocking rises up to four times above extensive grazing, reaching 4.3 cows ha-1 in a Colombian Leucaena system that eliminated chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Milk rose 29% on high tree-density pasture against low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture against full sun, with dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Under drought, forage held constant in a Colombian silvopastoral system while grass-monoculture biomass fell to 25 %, deep-rooted trees give steadier dry-season forage, cattle are better fed in critical drought periods, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades (440 mm) [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal tied to tree density: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture (1110 trees/ha) gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field, while the low-density stand (407 trees/ha) gave 16.6 L [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Not every comparison finds a milk gain: a systematic review of mostly Brazilian dairy silvopasture found that the studies which measured milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture, even where trees altered the thermal environment [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. What separates that null from the gains, as far as the evidence says, is the system: the gains come mostly from intensive silvopasture with fodder shrubs such as Leucaena and Tithonia, where the trees add feed as well as shade, while the Brazilian studies compare shade from exotic trees against treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Apart from that review, every unit is an earlier study read second-hand through a FAO country assessment, Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume, and none is a pastoral-system experiment run by the citing authors [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3]. The Senegalese diet shares describe how much of the ration comes from trees, not a measured production change [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Most of the Latin American evidence is intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs in upper-middle-income Colombia, the Brazilian review is upper-middle income, and the Costa Rican units are high-income; milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The El Hatico result is a single farm compared year on year, and the Colombian drought-forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade trees have been found to raise output, to lower the main-crop yield, and to make no difference. On the gain side, a global coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield, bean size and quality (SMD = +0.42) [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, leguminous shade trees and low canopy openness generally benefited yields, and leguminous shade strongly raised yields at high canopy openness in the shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than monocultures, and a review citing Pérez-Neira et al. reports total agroforestry production three times that of monocultures [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to or 3% higher than full sun (Pinoargote et al. 2016) [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]; shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]; nitrogen fixed in coffee under Erythrina poeppigiana or Inga edulis is around 100 kg ha-1 (Leblanc et al. 2007) [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12]; and shade trees are cited as reducing the biennial swing in coffee yields and, in other studies, lowering yield variability under more diverse shade [ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the loss side, the same cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, a shaded coffee and cocoa meta-analysis found productivity per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and reviews cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures (Armengot et al. 2016), coffee yield 30% lower once shade was established (Siles et al.), and coffee fruit production 41% lower under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade than under at most 20% cover (Estivariz 1997) [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]. Coffee yields declined under >60% shade from reduced light and humidity-linked disease, high cocoa yield (> 1.5 t/ha) is only possible below 100-150 t C/ha of carbon storage, and shade trees can harm cocoa under severe drought, depending on species (Abdulai et al. 2018), as can tree–cacao water competition (Blaser et al. 2018) [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_3, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. A further set of studies finds no difference: no yield effect of shade in a coffee case study, in shaded coffee under 30% cover in Costa Rica (Cerda et al. 2016) or in fruiting nodes of young shaded coffee (Angrand et al. 2004); no relation between shade and cocoa drought loss in Bahia or coffee hurricane loss in Chiapas; shade not preventing the drought yield decline in a Ghana cocoa experiment or showing a benefit in Ethiopia's extreme shock; and no soil nitrogen difference across cocoa systems [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides is largely what is counted and how much shade there is. Counting the main crop alone, cocoa and coffee yields are usually lower under shade; counting the whole system, including timber, fruit and other by-crops, output is higher — the same cocoa meta-analysis reports both, as does the review citing total production [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]. Revenue can offset the yield gap: the review reporting cocoa 41% higher in monocultures adds that agroforestry revenues compensate economically for the difference [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6]. Shade level is the second separator: 30 to 60% shade gave the most favourable coffee results and yields declined above 60%, moderate shade matched full sun, and the 41% coffee fruit loss came at 40 to 60% Erythrina cover against at most 20% [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]; but the coffee meta-analysis found that no moderator, shade density included, explained a statistically significant share of the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy openness are therefore the design questions, and management intensity can matter more than shade itself [ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Under shocks the evidence leans to no shade effect either way [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Many units are earlier studies repeated in Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews and a CATIE edited volume; the coffee, cocoa and shaded coffee-and-cocoa meta-analyses are the main syntheses [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. The nitrogen units are soil-fertility components, not yield measures, and the Paraná result depends on tree species and development [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the system-production and yield-variability statements; located evidence spans low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana, upper-middle-income Brazil and Mexico and high-income Costa Rica, so the transfer to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems is adjacent [ev_crop_yield_morel24_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In high-income settings, agroforestry has been found both to raise and to lower output. Gains: in subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]; cited studies from Cañas, Costa Rica found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than in full sun and dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]; and a cited Costa Rican study found moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to, or 3% higher than, full sun [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]. Losses: a cited Costa Rican experiment recorded a 30% coffee yield reduction in the shaded system against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: What separates the sides is the system and the competition for resources. The gains are livestock under tree cover and windbreak-sheltered vegetables in Ontario, where the plots were irrigated from ditches, whereas the losses are crops competing with trees: cereal next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts and established shade over coffee [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. Distance from the trees and the season separate them within the shelterbelt study: yields were depressed next to the belt every year, higher in the sheltered zone in 1989 and 1990, and showed no sheltered gain in the wet 1991 season [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Costa Rican coffee several units find no difference: a case study recorded no negative yield effect of shade, systems under 30 % shade cover did not differ in yield from full sun with management intensity driving yield instead, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]. All units are from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; most are earlier findings read second-hand through reviews, while the Ontario result was measured directly but at a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt units were measured in the field; their net loss uses the mid-field yield as the reference, a baseline the authors question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The coffee units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: The units in this mixed-income cell measure different things and point different ways. A meta-analysis of shaded against conventional (unshaded) coffee and cocoa found productivity per hectare 26% lower in the shaded systems (p < 0.001) [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows on sloping farmland found they significantly raised soil total nitrogen against farmland without hedgerows (standardized mean difference 1.33, 95% CI 0.98–1.68), soil nitrogen being read here as a component of the production gap [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates them is both the practice and the outcome: the yield fall is the crop-specific cost of shade in perennial tree crops, measured as the crop harvest itself [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1], while the gain is a soil-fertility component under contour hedgerows, not a measured yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The hedgerow pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows (vetiver and switchgrass alongside Leucaena, Gliricidia and Calliandra), so it is not woody-hedgerow-specific evidence [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The shaded-crop unit is registered under a different source id but its file is the Jezeer et al. meta-analysis [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. For a project these readings are not interchangeable: higher soil nitrogen does not say that harvests rise, and lower shaded-crop yield per hectare does not count the other products of the shade trees.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, studies disagree on whether agroforestry narrows the production gap: livestock and sheltered-crop systems mostly gain, while crops intercropped with trees often lose output. Gains: wheat and barley intercropped 2.5 m from trees in Iran out-yielded monocultures by 35% and 39% [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]; a meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland, alongside microclimatic improvements [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]; tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian cactus pear and buffel grass system [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]; and on the livestock side, Brazilian silvopasture gave higher daily bodyweight gain per animal, Colombian intensive silvopasture gave 32.1% more milk than the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, stocking reached 4.3 cows ha-1 while chemical fertiliser was eliminated, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Under drought, forage in a Colombian silvopastoral system stayed constant while grass monoculture biomass fell to 25%, deep-rooted trees give more stable dry-season forage, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades at 440 mm [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Losses: intercropped wheat in China and maize in Indonesia yielded significantly less than monocultures, and Brazilian soybean gave about 500 and 700 kg ha-1 against about 3000 and 2700 kg ha-1 in monoculture, attributed to lower radiation [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]; in a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, soybean intercropped between juvenile plumcot rows yielded 46.03% less than sole-cropped soybean and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; and dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. In perennial crops, shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded monoculture control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a coconut review reports, second-hand, increased nut yields when pasture, black pepper and coffee were intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: Gains and losses both carry material weight, so no direction is stated; what separates them is visible in the evidence. Production system: the livestock and silvopasture units are almost all gains, while the losses are concentrated in crops intercropped with trees, where shading and competition reduce the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]; the Chinese plumcot losses were measured with the crop rows only about a metre from young trees [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Distance and density: within one Chinese meta-analysis, yield rose across sheltered farmland but fell in the edge zone next to the trees, and the figures are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; in Colombia, dense Acacia lowered milk per cow while sparser planting raised it [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Management: the soybean loss is attributed to radiation, which the authors tie to pruning and management of the system [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. For a Task Team Leader, the actionable distinctions are system type, tree spacing and density, and canopy management. On evidence quality, the plumcot intercrop is a direct randomised trial, while most other units on both sides are earlier results cited in Portuguese- or Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the shelterbelt meta-analysis is the main primary synthesis and supplies one figure on each side [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. The nitrogen unit is a soil-fertility component rather than a yield measure [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7], and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year, with the Colombian forage result likely describing the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Some silvopasture evidence also finds no difference: a systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, reports that the studies that evaluated milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Under shocks the perennial-crop evidence finds no shade effect either way: cocoa yield loss in the Bahian drought was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover, and Mexican coffee farms lost 18 to 40% of their harvest after a hurricane regardless of vegetation management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Paraná coffee result depends on tree species and development, and the coffee and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].

agroforestry__recurrent_cost.mechanism: Running a multi-component tree system costs more each year than a single crop because the tree, fruit-tree and crop components each need inputs. In a long-running trial on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, the cost of production was the largest in the Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system, at 482 USD ha−1 yr−1, against 168 for sole pigeon pea [ev_project_cost_biswas22_1].
agroforestry__recurrent_cost.conditionality: This is a single research-station trial, so confidence is very low; the cost class (large) is set against the LIC/LMIC context, not against other studies [ev_project_cost_biswas22_1]. The yearly cost is averaged over the full cycle and mixes establishment items (seedlings, grafts, irrigation at establishment) with recurrent ones (fertiliser, pesticide, labour), so it overstates the running cost once the trees are established. The higher cost buys more products: the same system also carried tree and fruit output that sole pigeon pea does not, so the cost alone says nothing about profitability. India is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in low-income Burkina Faso, not measured damage, and the rating itself describes good coping [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: Fire is named among the factors behind the lack of regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, alongside climate change, grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Fire is among several listed threats and its separate effect is not measured; the parkland unit is from lower-middle-income Senegal, within the LIC/LMIC target, and concerns long-term parkland persistence [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Both units are practitioner judgements on documented technology sheets, not measured damage, from regeneration practices in low-income Burkina Faso and lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, about local windstorms rather than cyclones, with no measured damage, so it does not show the regenerated trees are undamaged [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind damage to regenerated trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates gains in animal and habitat diversity, its compiler noting that many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites and that, compared with degraded sites, FMNR sites provide more habitats in the trees or soil [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Niger's Maradi region, FMNR adoption appears to raise tree diversity by between one and three species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare compared with matched non-adopters [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.conditionality: The Kenyan units come from a WOCAT technology sheet for FMNR in lower-middle-income Kenya and are compiler judgements comparing regenerated with degraded sites, not species surveys [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. The Niger result is a matched comparison of adopters with non-adopters that counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. The evidence comes from a narrow base in Kenya and Niger, so confidence is medium.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.mechanism: In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.conditionality: Two literature units measure soil carbon under trees (a component of sequestration), and the Humbo figure is a project total from a World Vision self-evaluation with no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The literature is from semi-arid West Africa and Ethiopia (low- and lower-middle-income countries) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a measured stock or rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Measured directly on Ethiopian wheat farms, soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside the Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of the 2013 cropping season, so the cited 46 per cent canopy gain was not reproduced at that site; this null lowers the agreement rather than the class [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.mechanism: A review reports that Ilstedt et al., combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective; recharge is read here as a component of catchment water yield [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect for this cell: it is one modelling result read second-hand, with no measured finding and no country, and it points to an intermediate optimum rather than more trees always raising recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. A second independent source or one measured finding on water yield or recharge under regenerated farmland trees would let the cell state a class.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one lower-middle-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_1]. The same quote notes FMNR in Ghana cost less per household than tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, mainly FMNR, cost $58 per hectare [ev_project_cost_crs23_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per hectare where at least one practice was adopted, from one lower-middle-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_2]. The same quote gives $1,387 per hectare for tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement, and neither unit puts a size on the drought benefit [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Only the Sahelian parkland unit is recorded in an agro-pastoral system; the Kenyan rating is applied here by default [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. With two units, one a review citation and one a rating, the cell lacks any measured drought loss with and without trees.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: Apart from the Ethiopian paired-plot study, which is a drought-year result reported as an 'up to' figure with its normal-season gain reported separately [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2], the literature units are reviews citing earlier work, and the deep-water unit enters as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating of a slight benefit on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Parkland hydraulic redistribution lets crops use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3], and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The Ethiopian paired-plot study is the measured result here: a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, with the normal-season gain reported separately in the same study [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. The other literature unit is a review describing a soil-water process in West African Sahel parklands, used as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR unit is a single compiler rating of a slight benefit, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: In Senegal's sylvopastoral zone, tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet in the run-up to the rains [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The Senegal diet-share estimate is a second-hand figure entering as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating of a slight benefit, not a measurement, and is applied to pastoral rangeland by default [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Honduran point is an earlier observation cited in an ICRAF working paper, and it does not come from a pastoral rangeland system, so it is applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: Two sources point to a slight reduction in drought damage. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as decreased, its compiler judging that FMNR improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The cell is thin: one compiler judgement on a WOCAT technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts] and one promoter-written practitioner account from Honduras. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. Neither unit puts a size on the benefit or measures drought losses with and without the practice in a controlled comparison; an independent measured study is what is missing.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__est.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__est.conditionality: The figure is a programme cost per adopting household, not a per-hectare establishment cost, so it fits this indicator only loosely and comes from one country arm [ev_project_cost_crs23_1]. The same quote notes FMNR in Ghana cost less per household than tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.mechanism: The only evidence is the compiler of the Kenyan WOCAT sheet on Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who comments that tree cover can increase the risk of major wildfires and advises fire breaks for larger FMNR sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in lower-middle-income Kenya, not a measured change in fire occurrence or damage [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.mechanism: The only evidence is the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who states that it also mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.conditionality: This is a single compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
