The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates flood impacts as decreased, its compiler noting that FMNR also mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the cell rests on a single compiler judgement on a WOCAT technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya, not a measured reduction in flood damage; a further independent source or a measured finding is what is missing [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__foo.mechanism: Farmer-managed natural regeneration improves food security modestly. Across World Vision FMNR project endlines, participants had 0.26 fewer months of food shortage than non-participants, and in Senegal's southern-centre groundnut basin 3 % of FMNR adopters against 14 % of non-adopters went more than 4 months without meeting their annual food needs (0 % against 4% in the northern-centre basin) [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Talensi, Ghana, between the 2017 baseline and the 2020 endline the share of households with sufficient diet diversity rose from 44.5% to 55.8% and the share with one or more hungry months fell from 68.2% to 41% [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet records higher food security and self-sufficiency, its compiler noting that more diversified livelihoods reduce the risk of food insecurity [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__foo.conditionality: In Maradi, Niger, a matched comparison found that FMNR did not appear to reduce the number of months of perceived food shortage [ev_food_security_haglund11_1]. The World Vision results are self-evaluations, the brief stating that the FMNR effect cannot be fully separated from other project activities, and the Talensi figures are a before-and-after survey with no control group and a change in sampling [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. The Senegal shares come from an English abstract inside a French volume with no stated significance test [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a household survey result [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside, and access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: The Senegal units come from a review citing earlier studies and the Sahelian parkland figure is likewise a cited result; the temperature figures are canopy measurements, and the productivity gain is stated without a size [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Parkland trees cool crops and livestock: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside, and access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: The Ethiopian cooling was measured directly on farm; the other units are reviews citing earlier studies, and all report canopy temperature or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. The yield link is modelled rather than measured, and the model's null without applied N is the no-benefit result that discounts the class: on unfertilised wheat the cooling did not carry through to simulated yield [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Faidherbia albida parkland trees on Ethiopian wheat farms lowered midday air temperature by up to 6°C against the open field: it peaked at 36 °C in the open and at 29 °C under the canopy, and exceeded 28 °C for about six hours a day in the open against less than two hours under the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A crop model in the same study found that this cooling raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: Without applied N, simulated wheat yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature, so the benefit depends on fertilisation; this modelled null is the no-benefit result that discounts the class [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. All units come from a single Ethiopian on-farm study in low-income rainfed cropping, within the LIC/LMIC target; the cooling was measured, the yield response modelled [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Faidherbia albida parkland trees on Ethiopian wheat farms lowered midday air temperature by up to 6°C, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C in the open field, and in Senegal's Ferlo air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: These are temperature measurements under tree canopies (the Ethiopian one measured on farm, the Senegalese and Sahelian ones cited from earlier studies), linked to heat stress through microclimate buffering rather than a measured heat-stress outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. They come from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal and the wider Sahel [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__pro.mechanism: Millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, a cited meta-analysis reports mean yield increases of 150 per cent for maize and 73 per cent for sorghum under its canopy, and millet and groundnut yields were higher in plots with intensive FMNR [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Shrubs on Sudano-Sahelian fields often raised millet and sorghum yields (−25 to + 120%), and soil nitrogen was higher beneath shrubs and Faidherbia albida canopies, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__pro.conditionality: Groundnut under Faidherbia albida behaved variably and groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata, so the effect depends on which trees are retained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11]. The pooled magnitude draws on two soil-nitrogen percentages and an Ethiopian drought-season wheat gain reported as "up to" 85% [ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2], and the Ghana figure is a share of households reporting higher yield [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__rur.mechanism: Senegalese households practising intensive FMNR gain on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber products against 29.73 USD for others, the annual value of FMNR in Niger through soil fertility, firewood and fodder was calculated at US$56 per hectare, and FMNR project participants were 15 percent points more likely to report higher household income [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet records higher farm income, its compiler crediting additional sources of income from the sale of wood, honey, medicinal components and non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. Across World Vision FMNR projects, participant households were nine percentage points more likely than non-participants to report a decrease in poverty in their communities, reported similarly by poorer and female-headed households [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. In Maradi, Niger, FMNR adoption increased gross annual household income by between 46 and 56 USD per capita compared with propensity-matched non-adopters, and the annual benefit-cost ratio of practising FMNR was estimated at between 2.5 and 3.0 [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1]. In south-central Niger, sales of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR raise the income of all social categories, even the vulnerable and very vulnerable, and the net present value of FMNR at 10% over 20 years was €772 per hectare [ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, from the first year onwards Quesungual farmers can rent their plots for livestock grazing because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__rur.conditionality: Several units are World Vision self-evaluations or figures cited in them, and the social return on investment is a monetised social-value construct [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. The WOCAT farm-income unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a household survey result [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. The World Vision poverty result is a self-reported community perception, and the brief states FMNR cannot be fully separated from other project activities [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. The Maradi income and benefit-cost figures come from a matched survey comparison, while the fuelwood and net-present-value figures are cited in a grey-literature review [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. The Honduran grazing-rent point is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no income figure, for a system bundled with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_household_income_welc02_7].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__soi.mechanism: Across World Vision FMNR projects, participants were 10 percent points more likely than non-participants to report a reduction in erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__soi.conditionality: The World Vision result is a reported perception from a self-evaluation in which the FMNR effect cannot be fully separated from other project activities [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Honduran landslide result is an earlier observation cited in a working paper, for a slash-and-mulch system under very intense rainfall [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates reduced downstream siltation, its compiler noting that less wind and water erosion reduces the siltation of ponds and water pans [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.conditionality: The cell rests on a single compiler judgement from a technology sheet in lower-middle-income Kenya, with no measurement behind it; siltation enters as a component of water-quality risk, and no unit measures water quality itself [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. What is missing is a measured sediment or water-quality comparison downstream of regenerated farmland against comparable farmland without regeneration, or a second independent source; this is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of no effect.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.mechanism: Studies of trees on regenerated farmland disagree on soil water, so no direction is stated. On the side of more water stress, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field, while the authors observed no variation in topsoil moisture content between treatments [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the side of less, in Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet also points that way, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.conditionality: The sides differ in system and in what is measured. The Ethiopian result is a measured subsoil draw-down under heavily pruned parkland trees with a growing wheat crop [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; the Honduran result is driest-month soil humidity in a slash-and-mulch system against slash-and-burn, which the authors credit to soil cover and soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]; and the WOCAT unit speaks of groundwater, not crop-root-zone moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet rather than a soil-moisture measurement [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Whether pruning or tree density changes the subsoil draw-down is not tested [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The cited parkland tree-density result for groundwater recharge sits in the regeneration catchment water yield row.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__win.mechanism: Practitioner ratings on WOCAT sheets for regeneration practices in Burkina Faso and Kenya record reduced wind speed, the Kenyan compiler noting that FMNR trees serve as a windbreak protecting houses, greenhouses and crop fields against heavy winds [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1358_2017_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_507_2019_wind_velocity].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__win.conditionality: Both units are compiler judgements of wind speed on documented technology sheets for regeneration practices in low-income Burkina Faso and lower-middle-income Kenya, not measured storm or cyclone losses [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1358_2017_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_507_2019_wind_velocity].

agroforestry__rural_poverty.mechanism: Household income and economic return are used as proxies for rural poverty [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. Across sub-Saharan Africa, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that agroforestry adoption raises income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001) [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. Gains include Senegalese FMNR households earning more from non-timber products than non-adopters, calliandra fodder raising dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda, and a windbreak hedge in Senegalese irrigated rice with an internal rate of return of 36 per cent [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1, ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet records higher farm income, its compiler crediting additional sources of income from the sale of wood, honey, medicinal components and non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. Across World Vision FMNR projects, participant households were nine percentage points more likely than non-participants to report a decrease in poverty in their communities, reported similarly by poorer and female-headed households [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. In Rwanda, food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In Maradi, Niger, FMNR adoption increased gross annual household income by between 46 and 56 USD per capita compared with propensity-matched non-adopters, and the annual benefit-cost ratio of practising FMNR was estimated at between 2.5 and 3.0 [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1]. In south-central Niger, sales of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR raise the income of all social categories, even the vulnerable and very vulnerable, and the net present value of FMNR at 10% over 20 years was €772 per hectare [ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system, and producer income from milk sales was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture owing to a higher carrying capacity [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1], a case cited second-hand found a coffee price crash cut sun-coffee net revenue far more than that of extensive agroforestry [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found smaller losses for high-shade systems under a 50% coffee price fall [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2]. Field trials of trees with crops add returns from several systems. In south-western Nigeria, net present values of a young sweet orange orchard were N -37900 monocropped against N 154300 intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus, N 105900 with cassava and maize and N -300 with egusi melon then soyabeans, because the intercropped plots yielded revenue throughout while the monocrop earned nothing in the first two years [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. In Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal plantation earned more net revenue per hectare than sole crops: 558 against 501 SDG for sorghum, 300 against 205 for sesame and 518 against 389 for roselle [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]. In Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave net benefits of 4148 against 2386 US$ per hectare for the traditional treeless system, the only alternative not dominated in the trial [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]. On degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, net returns of a Gmelina–mango–pigeon pea system were 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a decade, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]; in Haryana, India, eucalyptus boundary strips gave a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 over the first rotation (Ram et al. 2011, reported in a review) [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia mulch grown within the coffee gave the largest gross margins and returns to labour and the most favourable benefit–cost ratio (5.5) [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. In Nigeria, maize mulched with tree prunings returned higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer or no input when the land for the trees was not valued [ev_economic_return_korm99_5]; in Xinjiang, China, plumcot intercrops had a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops in the establishment years [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]; in West Java, Indonesia, a study by Rahman et al. (2017), cited in a systematic review, found agroforestry systems compared well with swidden cultivation on net present value and benefit-cost ratio [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2]; and in the East Usambara Mountains of Tanzania, cash-crop revenues and total income were significantly higher under improved agroforestry than under traditional methods [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, from the first year onwards Quesungual farmers can rent their plots for livestock grazing because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7].
agroforestry__rural_poverty.conditionality: Results are mixed: one systematic review's pooled income effect is small and not statistically significant, though the more recent sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds a significant one [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]; crop–fruit tree intercropping in China lowered gross household income, silvopasture income lags traditional pasture in the first years, and Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2, ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6]. Several gains are self-evaluations, bundled-project results or a modelled business case, and the proxies measure income or returns rather than poverty itself [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]. The WOCAT farm-income unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a household survey result [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing, because many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects could not be separated from drought and other climatic events [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. The World Vision poverty result is a self-reported community perception from participants [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Maradi income and benefit-cost figures come from a matched survey comparison, while the fuelwood and net-present-value figures are cited in a grey-literature review [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. The Zambian loss comparison and Mozambique result are earlier findings cited in a working paper and a review [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1, ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Colombian ratio and milk-income figures are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language systematic review and a CATIE edited volume [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. The shaded coffee and cocoa evidence also pulls both ways: in Guayas, Ecuador, technified cacao monoculture earned a higher net margin per hectare than organic or traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2], a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]; these units are crop-specific, and the price-fall result is modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2]. The new trial evidence shows what separates gains from losses. Land and labour: cut-and-carry tree mulch for maize is only profitable in land- and labour-abundant areas, and where land is scarce it is unprofitable in the short and long term, with marginal returns below zero [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. Input costs: in West Bengal the benefit-cost ratio was higher for sole pigeon pea than for pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, even though the full tree system earned more in total [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2, ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. Time: the orchard and plumcot results are establishment-period returns, in which the crops pay while the trees are young [ev_household_income_aiyel01_4, ev_economic_return_wang23_1], and the Indian net return depends on a timber harvest in the final year [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. The Tanzanian comparison bundles trees with cash crops and cattle, and its improved farms also carried higher household overhead costs and hired more labour, so the income gain is not the trees' alone [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan meta-analysis rests mostly on adopter-versus-non-adopter contrasts in Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The trial budgets (Nigeria, Sudan, Cameroon, India, China) are researcher-run plots priced at local markets, not household poverty measures, and the Xinjiang result is from an irrigated upper-middle-income system [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The Honduran grazing-rent point is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no income figure, for a system bundled with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_household_income_welc02_7].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage review cites a study by Ram et al. finding a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, with returns from fodder, wood or fibre after only an initial investment [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese and Indian figures are earlier studies read second-hand in reviews, and the Indian ratio is expected to rise in later rotations because coppiced Eucalyptus costs little to regrow [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. The Chinese trial covers only the establishment years, and in the same trial the intercropped soybean and alfalfa yielded much less than sole crops, so the cash-flow gain comes from the fruit trees rather than from the crop [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The evidence comes from lower-middle-income Senegal and India and upper-middle-income China.

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In Senegal's southern-centre groundnut basin, households practising intensive FMNR earned on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber products against 29.73 USD for other households [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: Income and returns stand in for poverty here rather than measuring it, and the strength of the effect is not quantified against a poverty measure. The Senegal figures are an adopter versus non-adopter survey comparison with no stated significance test, taken from an English abstract inside a French volume, and the Malawian ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data rather than measured household income [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. The FMNR and Tephrosia results come from different sub-practices, regeneration-based farmland in Senegal and a planted relay intercrop in Malawi, which agree in direction only.

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers, and tree density was positively associated with food security in some agroecologies [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: The Rwandan effect varied by agroecology: more trees went with higher food security in Congo Nile but lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales and flood-fruit findings are farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. Household income, wealth and food security are used here as proxies for rural poverty, and the Rwandan units are cross-sectional associations rather than a comparison during a shock [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: Returns in tree-perennial agroforestry have been reported both above and below the alternative. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was almost twice as high in agroforestry systems as in monocultures [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. In a Brazilian system at Tomé-Açu, the rice component showed negative economic performance and black pepper was unprofitable in low-price cycles [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: The two units measure different things: the Bolivian gain is a whole-system return per day of labour against monoculture, while the Brazilian loss is the performance of single components, which the authors say need adjustment in production, technology or management, and which depends on price cycles [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. Component choice and exposure to price swings are therefore what a project would need to check. Both units are reviews citing earlier studies with no effect sizes and measure returns as a proxy, not poverty; they come from Bolivia (lower-middle income) and Brazil (upper-middle) [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.mechanism: Agroforestry adds income and food through tree products and yields: FMNR in Niger is valued at US$56 per hectare a year in soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, FMNR-adopting households in Senegal earn 72.65 USD per season from non-timber products against 29.73 USD for others, and calliandra fodder raises farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda by about US$ 101–122 a year by replacing dairy meal [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Food-security gains include a dietary diversity score raised by 1.22 under Vi Agroforestry advice in Kenya, food crop value raised by 35% by fertilizer trees in Malawi, fewer months of food shortage among FMNR participants, and diet diversity rising with use of tree products [ev_food_security_castle21s_1, ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A systematic review concludes that incomes improved through higher yields, payments for ecosystem services or higher prices from eco-certification [ev_t6_income_pathway_castle21_5].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.conditionality: The pooled income effect is small and not significant (0.12 SMD, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.30), the meta-analysis ratios for revenue, profit and benefit-cost are not significant, and several units are null: tree-product income per household stayed at USD 82 PPP, food-insecurity scores barely changed, income change was not expected within the programme period, and improved fallows did not translate into household welfare on small farms [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_2, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_3, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_food_security_rgaf23_9, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_household_income_place05_2]. One unit points the other way: in Uganda, FMNR participants, who were often the poorer households, were less likely to report income gains [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. All evidence is from LIC/LMIC settings, but most units measure proxies for poverty (income, returns, food security) rather than poverty itself, and some results are bundled project outcomes or modelled scenarios, such as the Talensi diet and hungry-month changes and a Nigerian climate model [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_food_security_castle21s_1, ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.mechanism: Household income and economic returns stand in for poverty in this evidence, and they move in both directions. Gains: an integrative review of Brazilian family-farm agroforestry viability studies found all indices positive, with internal rates of return always above 7% and benefit-cost ratios above 1, most between 1.20 and 2.50 and some above 3.00; individual systems in Pará reached a benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 and an internal rate of return of 15%, or cleared a 10% hurdle rate [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_2, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8]. In Colombia, silvopasture raised income through better animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and higher carrying capacity: a Bank-commissioned business case estimates up to US$523/ha more annual income with production costs US$127/ha lower, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34, milk-sale income was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture, and Caquetá farms in silvopastoral projects saw higher income from animal sales [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1, ev_household_income_bur24_1]. A Brazilian review also cites potential to raise profitability in municipalities prone to climate variation [ev_economic_return_ribeiro22_2]. Losses: crop–fruit tree intercropping in Xinjiang, China lowered gross household income (−0.29 SMD) [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; silvopasture income lags traditional pasture in the first years after establishment [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]; an organic agroforestry system in Paraná collapsed from the seventh year through lack of long-term management and planning, the rice component at Tomé-Açu lost money and black pepper did so in low-price cycles, and a multistrata coconut, lemon, passionfruit, cowpea and cassava system gave the lowest return of those assessed [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_9]. For Indonesian social-forestry permits, profitability was no better for permit holders than for households without one [ev_economic_return_castle21s_4].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.conditionality: What separates the sides, where the evidence says: time since establishment, since silvopasture income lags in the early years and the Colombian completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing because many systems were still being established and effects could not be separated from drought [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]; long-term management and planning, the stated cause of the Paraná collapse [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5]; the choice of components and their prices, with rice and black pepper losing and one multistrata mix earning least [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_9]; and system type, with the Colombian silvopasture gains set against the Xinjiang crop–fruit tree intercropping loss [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. For a Task Team Leader the practical points are to plan for an establishment-period income gap and to vet component choice and long-term management. On evidence quality, the gain side leans on grey-literature Brazilian viability studies, earlier results cited in reviews, a modelled business case for the US$523/ha figure, and a brief with no effect size [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1, ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]; the Xinjiang loss is a quantified estimate from a systematic review, while the other losses are narrative case reports. All units measure income or returns rather than poverty itself.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, the El Niño drought of 2015 and 2016 killed 15% of cocoa trees against under 1% normally and 7% of the 317 woody shade trees, with no shade-tree species particularly affected; potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, and was still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The engine sets the threat class at high, but the whole row is one observational study of one drought event in Bahia [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. It has no unshaded comparator, so it shows the damage to the shaded system, not that shade caused it. Cocoa units are crop-specific and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil is upper-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1]. No second independent drought study of a shaded perennial system is in the pool, and none from a low- or lower-middle-income country.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: A tropics review, citing earlier studies, reports that flooding increases tree mortality in cacao agroforests, with older systems potentially more vulnerable [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The two units point different ways: a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2], while the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. Both are second-hand readings and crop-specific, entering under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; neither measures how much damage a flood does. India is lower-middle income [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: In shaded coffee in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, a field study found minimal vegetation damage as a result of the hurricane, and no small landslides within the study plots [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports, citing earlier work, that the coconut palm can withstand natural calamities like typhoons and flooding [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The measured finding comes from a single hurricane whose winds the unit records as mild, so it does not show shaded perennials withstand a severe cyclone [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]. The coconut statement is a second-hand review claim about the palm itself, not a measurement [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]. Both are crop-specific and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Mexico is upper-middle income and India lower-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__biodiver.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa hold species that sun plantations lose. A global meta-analysis of coffee and cacao by De Beenhouwer et al. found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest under a diverse, mostly indigenous shade canopy was compared with plantation under sparse shade of one or a few tree species; the structurally complex canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports, from Gordon et al. (2007), bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Nicaraguan coffee, most certification schemes had a tree-diversity index, used as a proxy for habitat quality, that rose against non-certified farms [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__biodiver.conditionality: The gains are measured against sun or sparse-shade plantations. Against natural forest, agroforest held 11% fewer species in total and 35% fewer forest species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]; that marks a ceiling, since shade cropping replaces plantation or farmland rather than forest, not a loss caused by the practice. The other harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Scheme design matters: C.A.F.E. Practices was the only Nicaraguan certification scheme under which tree diversity fell [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The bird figure and the Nicaraguan result are second-hand readings, and the review notes the shaded coffee systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The coffee and cacao meta-analysis draws on Latin America, Asia and Africa, most of it Latin American [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. The cocoa and coffee units from single crops enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__carbon_s.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee, cocoa and coconut store more carbon in biomass, and in some studies soil, than the crop grown alone. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry, including cocoa and shade trees, is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. East African perennial tree-crop systems hold 29.9 Mg C ha−1 of above-ground carbon, and modelled Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee systems translate to biomass carbon of 139.5 and 153.4 Mg/ha [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. A coconut review reports carbon storage by coconut palms in mixed stands is clearly greater than in sole stands, especially when the mix involves trees, and higher soil carbon sequestration in mixed-species systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kumar22_1]; a coffee review reports soil organic matter improved by 20–35% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5]. Against these removals, a global synthesis of agroforestry greenhouse-gas data found that net soil methane (CH4) emissions increased when agriculture changed to shaded perennial-crop systems, whereas they fell under improved fallow and tree plantations on arable land [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__carbon_s.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class: what is missing is a net balance. The carbon figures count storage in biomass and soil only, while the methane finding points the other way for this very family, and no unit puts carbon removals and methane (or nitrous oxide) together in one CO2-equivalent account [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. This is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of no effect. The carbon side is itself uneven: the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1], certified shade coffee in Nicaragua showed gains in above-ground carbon stocks that were not statistically significant [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1], and the East African and Ethiopian figures are stocks, not annual rates, the Ethiopian ones being cited model outputs [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The methane result rests on few observations for shaded perennial-crop systems and carries no size [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. The Costa Rican coffee units are from a high-income country [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. What would let the cell state a class is a whole-system greenhouse-gas balance (carbon stored in biomass and soil, net of methane and nitrous oxide) for shaded coffee, cocoa or coconut against the unshaded crop.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.mechanism: In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii between rows of smallholder coffee and using it as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management because it reduced weeding, with benefit–cost ratios between 3.4 and 5.5 [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry against full-sun cocoa monocultures found that the higher total system production of agroforestry is not reflected in revenues, net present values or production costs: costs did not differ significantly between the systems [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.conditionality: The sources point in different directions for different reasons: the Rwandan saving comes from weed suppression by a mulch-producing legume intercrop, not from shade trees, while the cocoa meta-analysis compares shade-tree agroforestry with full-sun monoculture and finds no significant cost difference [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. Both are crop-specific (coffee and cocoa), from low- and lower-middle-income producing countries, and both concern recurrent production costs (labour, inputs), not establishment costs.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Reviews add that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
