The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: In a cocoa plantation in Ghana's Ashanti region, shade trees competed with cocoa for soil water through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought. All cocoa plants under the recommended leguminous shade tree Albizia ferruginea died; cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria, the most common shade tree, suffered 77% mortality and massive stress, with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun; and sap-flux recovery after the drought was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris. Soil water content was higher in full sun than under the shade trees, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: This is a single measured study on a single farm with a few replicate shade trees per species, so the row gives a direction only, with no size class [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The shade-tree species is part of the result: the loss was total under Albizia and heavy under Antiaris, so other shade species, densities or pruning regimes may behave differently. The drought was extreme; the same plots were also measured through wet and normal dry periods, which separates the drought response from ordinary shade effects [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The finding is crop-specific (cocoa) and enters under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; Ghana is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target. A financed shade-cocoa system in a drought-prone area carries this as a risk to the planted asset and the crop.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.mechanism: A review reports, second-hand, that coffee-based agroforestry in Mesoamerica can regulate ecological services including preventing flood occurrences, helping reduce the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: it is a single second-hand review sentence with no effect size, no country or income group, and a general claim about what coffee agroforestry can do rather than a measured flood outcome [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. A further independent source or a measured finding for shaded perennial systems is what is missing.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A coffee review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress (Lin et al. 2008; Meylan et al. 2017), and the IPCC notes, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not say how much that cuts crop losses. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. All are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]; and the review and IPCC statements are second-hand readings of earlier studies [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress, and the IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. All are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]; and the review and IPCC statements are second-hand readings of earlier studies [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa lower the temperature the crop experiences. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maxima and minima are buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], and a coffee review reports, citing Lin et al. 2008 and Meylan et al. 2017, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]; the same review cites shade trees improving microclimate stability in Central America (Perfecto and Armbrecht 2003) [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4], and the same tropical synthesis states, citing Avelino et al. 2011, that associated trees buffer air and soil temperature and raise humidity under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A CATIE volume reports, from earlier tropical studies, about 2°C cooling under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall compared with a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. The IPCC, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In a Ghanaian cocoa field study, the role of shade trees in moderating microclimate was confirmed especially in the dry and extremely dry periods, when daily mean maximum air temperatures were significantly higher, reaching up to 44°C, in the comparison with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not state how much that reduces crop or income losses, so the strength is not quantified and the class is slight. Reviews carry their own caveats in the same sentence: IPCC adds that the opposite of shade-tree cooling can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2], and the coffee review notes that in parts of East Africa excessive shade with heavy rain raised fungal infection risk (Jaramillo et al. 2009) [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee and cocoa and reports temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact, not crop losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. The same Ghanaian study is a caution on reading cooling as protection: the study notes record that its authors concluded the cooling did not protect the cocoa, because competition with the shade trees for soil water overrode it [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. The 50-year climate-change horizon in the CATIE quote is the cited authors' suggestion, not a measurement [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. The cocoa meta-analysis is weighted towards Ghana and the Ghanaian field study is from a single farm (both lower-middle income), the Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high income, and the reviews name no country, so the transfer to the LIC/LMIC target is adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains: a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield and bean quality (SMD = +0.42) against conventional systems [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures, and a Bolivian cocoa study cited second-hand found total production three times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; in Ethiopian smallholder coffee, leguminous shade and canopy openness benefited yields, including in the El Niño shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]; and second-hand reports cite moderate shade yielding up to 3% more than full-sun coffee, reduced biennial yield oscillation, lower yield variability under diverse shade, intercropped coconut yielding more nuts, nitrogen fixation around 100 kg ha-1 by Erythrina or Inga shade, and in Paraná shaded coffee yielding up to 101.99 kg/ha where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii in the alleys of smallholder coffee and applying it as mulch raised coffee yield by 23–36% over the trial, a further 25–42% when NPK fertilizer was added, though the gain was statistically significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1, ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2]. Losses: main-crop yield per hectare was 26% lower in shaded coffee and cocoa than conventional systems and cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; second-hand reports cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures, a 30% coffee yield reduction once shade was established, 41% fewer coffee fruits under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade, significant productivity reductions under Organic-certified shade coffee, and a cocoa yield ceiling at high carbon storage [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.conditionality: What separates the sides, in the sources' own terms, is first what is counted and second how much shade. The gains in total system output count the by-crops and timber, while the losses are in the main crop alone: the same cocoa meta-analysis reports cocoa yields 25% lower but total system yields about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Shade density: coffee yields declined under >60% shade with 30 to 60% shade most favourable, fruit set fell under 40 to 60% Erythrina cover, and shaded systems under 30 % cover did not differ from full sun, management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. Drought does not reliably favour shade: in the Ghanaian experiment shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2], cited work reports tree–cacao water competition pushing yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], Bahian cocoa drought losses were unrelated to shade-tree cover and Mexican hurricane harvest losses unrelated to shade management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6], and diverse shade showed no direct benefit in the El Niño shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Several units find no difference: in a Costa Rican case study no yield loss from shade was recorded, coconut yields are not strongly affected by interspace trees except where they block light, galangal yield was unaffected by over-canopy, soil nitrogen did not differ in cocoa systems, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]; the coffee meta-regression found no moderator, shade density included, that significantly explained the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut; the Rwandan Tephrosia gain comes from a mulch-producing legume intercrop rather than from shade trees [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]; the Ghanaian shade came from nets rather than trees, and the certification loss bundles shade with Organic certification rather than isolating it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. Many units are earlier studies read second-hand through Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.mechanism: Returns to farmers, used here as a proxy for rural poverty, tend to be higher in shaded coffee and cocoa. A meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems, with a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. Shade also cushions price shocks: in a case cited second-hand, a coffee price crash cut the net revenue of sun-grown coffee far more (30-fold) than of extensive agroforestry (2.9-fold) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found losses under a 50% coffee price fall were lower for high-shade and diversified systems, with high-shade low-investment farms holding a long-run net present value above zero where low-shade farms averaged one below zero [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2, ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was, by a cited study, almost twice as high in agroforestry as in monoculture, and in Paraná, Brazil a financial model found net present value and benefit-cost index always higher for shaded coffee [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1]. Among certified coffee farms in Nicaragua, C.A.F.E. Practices certification was associated with higher net income [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii grown as mulch within smallholder coffee gave the largest gross margins and returns to labour and the most favourable benefit-cost ratio (5.5) in the first season, from higher coffee yield and less weeding labour [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: in a farm survey in Guayas, Ecuador, technified monoculture earned the best net margin per hectare ($2323) against $1565 for organic and $484 for traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2]. Other units find no difference: a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]. What separates the sides is the comparison: the gains are against sun-grown or low-shade systems and under price shocks, while the losses are against an input-intensive technified monoculture. The certification result is bundled, crediting a certification scheme rather than shade alone [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1], the price-fall and net-present-value comparisons are modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1], and the Bolivian labour-return figure is read second-hand [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. The Rwandan result is from the first, unfertilised season of an on-farm trial, and Tephrosia there is a cut-back mulch shrub rather than a shade tree [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the Bolivian one, and the evidence mostly comes from upper-middle- and lower-middle-income producing countries, with low-income Rwanda the exception; returns are proxies for poverty, not poverty itself.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.mechanism: A pan-tropical meta-analysis found that soils in cocoa agroforestry systems have a significantly lower volumetric water content than full-sun cocoa monocultures, consistent with shade trees competing with cocoa for soil water [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. A field study on a cocoa farm in Ghana measured the same pattern: the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa led to higher water uptake and less soil water than under full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.conditionality: Size is not stated: the meta-analysis difference is not encoded and the Ghana study reports the direction only [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Both are crop-specific to cocoa, drawn mostly from lower-middle-income producing countries. Soil moisture enters as a component of water stress; in the Ghana study the lower soil water came with cocoa deaths under shade trees in an extreme drought, but the units here measure soil water, not crop water stress or yield loss directly [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: The row rests on one study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, which compared farms of differing vegetation management. It found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. For the farmer's harvest, shade trees made no measured difference.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: This is a no-mitigation result from the primary study. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, that more diverse coffee systems suffered less hurricane damage, was dropped from the evidence because the primary does not support it: the difference the study found was in landslides, not in the harvest. The 18 to 40% range is the loss across all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The unit is crop-specific (coffee) and counts because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it is a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and does not state the hurricane's severity [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: One study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Chiapas, Mexico, compared farms of differing vegetation management and found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms losing between 18 and 40% of harvest [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Shade trees did not reduce the hurricane's toll on the coffee harvest in that study.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: The row rests on the primary study's null result, so no mitigation of hurricane harvest loss in shaded coffee is established. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, reporting less damage in more diverse coffee systems, was dropped because the primary does not support it. The 18 to 40% range is the loss on all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The evidence is coffee-specific, counted under the ruling that shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, from a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In a severe drought, the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent across surveyed farms in a Colombian payment-for-ecosystem-services programme [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The loss is in the establishment phase: the source notes established systems were more resilient to drought than traditional pastures [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review, citing Vosti et al. (1998), states that accidental fire is a constant concern for silvopastoral producers because of the damage it could cause to trees and crops, and that post-fire re-establishment costs could be quite high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a second-hand comment on producer concern, not a measured loss, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review states that in the establishment phase of silvopastoral systems, tree seedlings must be protected from excess solar radiation and wind, as well as trampling, herbivory, weed competition and accidental fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one management statement, not a measured loss, wind is one of several establishment-phase threats, and the source is upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.mechanism: A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral systems against open pasture reports a pooled biodiversity log response ratio of 0.25 (a 28.4% difference), and the Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report attributes increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species, to silvopastoral systems at farm and landscape level [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. In the Colombian Amazon piedmont, silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, which enters as a forest-cover component [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.conditionality: The comparator matters: the meta-analysis gain is against open pasture, and the same table reports negative log response ratios for silvopasture compared with native forest, so the benefit applies where trees are added to treeless pasture, not where silvopasture replaces forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the measured project outcome is from upper-middle-income Colombia and the meta-analysis carries no income-group tag, so transfer to low-income pastoral systems is not established by these units [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. The Colombian bird and ant figures are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.mechanism: Colombian project measurements attribute net CO2 removals to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences and intensive silvopasture, and a preliminary balance reports that greater carbon capture and lower nitrogen losses in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. Spanish-language reviews add that silvopasture established from degraded woodland increases above- and below-ground carbon stocks and that tree-improved pastures and live fences scored as helping the mitigation pillar in a Colombian prioritisation [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in the Colombian Amazon piedmont, compared with control properties, also enters as a forest-cover component, with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.conditionality: The Colombian figure is a project total with no per-hectare or per-year denominator, and the other units are cited secondary or expert-prioritisation statements without rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and Latin America generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. The gain is mostly in tree biomass rather than soil: global meta-analyses find that converting pasture to agroforestry did not affect soil organic carbon stocks, and that silvopasture had the lowest increase or no change in soil carbon, because topsoil carbon under pasture already comes from perennial grass inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. Carbon removals from silvopasture therefore depend on how many trees are added and kept, not on soil gains.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.mechanism: A World Bank completion report for Colombia states that production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, attributing the saving to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower incidence of animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the figure is second-hand, an estimate the report takes from a Bank-commissioned business case rather than a measurement, and there is no other source to pool with [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. A further independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing. It comes from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and is a recurrent production-cost saving, not an establishment cost [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk production for agro-pastoralists during drought in a cited Zambian study [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among the services silvopasture can provide, without linking it to drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.conditionality: The Zambian unit is a review citing a single study, and the US unit is a background statement used as a soil-water component proxy for drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The US unit is high-income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; only the Zambian unit (low income) is from the target context [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. All units are from agro-pastoral systems [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and agroforestry in Brazil's semi-arid region had much less year-to-year variation in biomass productivity than conventional systems, attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.conditionality: The evidence is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the Zambian unit is low income, the Brazilian and Colombian units are upper-middle income, and the US unit is high income [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that in Brazil's semi-arid region agroforestry systems had lower year-to-year variation in biomass productivity over 4 years than conventional systems (for example 16% against 91% for maize plus bean), attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.conditionality: This single unit concerns yield stability, not a measured drought impact, and comes from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__pa.conditionality: The row rests on Latin American sources only, both upper-middle income or mostly so, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and all its units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review or a CATIE edited volume rather than new measurement [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought_haz.conditionality: Both are cited secondary findings without a drought effect size, and the Brazilian unit reports yield stability (coefficients of variation) rather than a drought-year comparison [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. Evidence is from low-income Zambia and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.mechanism: Silvopasture has been compared with forest and other unmanaged vegetation, not with open pasture. In Washington State, USA, silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth against non-grazed managed forest, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. Across six European Mediterranean countries, an overlay of burnt areas on land use found that, corrected for land-use extent, shrublands carried a greater share of fires than forest, grassland and agroforestry: agroforestry occupied 12% of the area and was associated with 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40% [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Agroforestry's lower share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2], and without the area correction the average fire incidents were lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class; the cell is data deficient. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]; the Mediterranean study compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. The nearest thing to the right comparator is grassland, and there the Mediterranean study found no significant difference, with grassland showing the lowest raw fire incidence [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: trees add woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces, and the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would then point to added risk [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. In the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. The Mediterranean overlay is observational and the agroforestry it maps is existing dehesa- and montado-type grazed wood-pasture, not new planting [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Both studies are from high-income settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.mechanism: Colombian silvopastoral soils eroded 35.3 percent less than degraded pasture in the Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent less in the flatter Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.conditionality: Both figures come from a single World Bank project report comparing silvopasture with degraded pasture rather than conventional pasture, and they measure erosion, a component of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.mechanism: Integrated agrosilvopastoral extension may improve diets: a systematic review cites a Kenyan study in which receiving Vi Agroforestry advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of the 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.conditionality: This cell is data deficient, not evidence of no effect. It rests on a single study reported second-hand in a review, from West Pokot, Kenya, and on extension advice rather than silvopasture measured on the farm [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. A second independent source, or the original study's own measurement, would let this cell state a class.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the shade-associated milk and weight-gain figures are associations rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that agroforestry systems in Brazil cut the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: This is one Brazilian study reported second-hand, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and it measures thermal comfort rather than livestock losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.mechanism: Trees in pasture have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains, mostly from Latin American intensive silvopasture and shaded pastures: Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, Brazilian silvopasture gave a higher mean bodyweight gain per animal (512 g day-1) than monoculture (452 g day-1), and tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian semi-arid system [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Losses come from a global quantitative review of dispersed trees in pasture: pasture yield fell by 20.8% on average against control plots, by a predicted 30% where tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, and to below 50% of the control under the oldest trees, while livestock yield fell by 18.6% on average, declining with more trees up to ~300 trees per hectare and with increasing tree age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.conditionality: The Brazilian and humid-tropic units are cited secondary results, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target; the nitrogen unit is a component rather than a productivity measure [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican units are high-income evidence, and the milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. What separates the sides: tree density and tree age, since in the review newly planted trees had no impact on pasture yield while dense and old stands cut it, and the dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture above also gave less milk than the open field [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]; and the system, since the gains are intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs or shaded pasture assessed on milk and weight gain, while the review pools paddock trees and silvopasture against treeless controls. Measured dairy evidence is thinner than the cited gains suggest: a systematic review of silvopasture for dairy cows, mostly from Brazil, found no significant difference in milk production between silvopastoral systems and treeless pasture in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Even in the review a third of livestock paddock years (33%) gained [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.mechanism: Silvopasture raised Colombian farmers' annual income by as much as US$523/ha in a Bank-commissioned business case, and participating Colombian Amazon farms saw higher income from animal sales [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system, and producer income from milk sales was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture owing to a higher carrying capacity [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.conditionality: Silvopasture income is lower than traditional pasture in the first years after establishment, and on a Nicaraguan farm its net income overtook pasture only in the fifth year [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_economic_return_diasf08_2]. The largest figure is a modelled upper bound, and the evidence is mainly from upper-middle-income Latin America, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1]. The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing, because many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects could not be separated from drought and other climatic events [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. The Colombian ratio and milk-income figures are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language systematic review and a CATIE edited volume [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.mechanism: Trees in pasture hold soil and water on the slope. In Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion, soils under silvopasture lost 12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha for degraded pasture, a mean reduction in erosion of 35.3 percent; in the flatter Cesar River Valley the figures were 17.5 against 18.5 t/ha [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. A review compiling field studies of agroforestry against its controls found that silvopastoral systems reduced soil loss by 68% and water loss by 73% on average [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.conditionality: Slope sets how much there is to gain: the Colombian reduction was large in the hilly Coffee Ecoregion and small in the flatter Cesar River Valley, where the project notes less scope for improvement [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The Colombian figures are project measurements against degraded pasture from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. The review percentages are simple averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, they mix temperate and tropical studies, and the review found no significant difference in soil-loss reduction between silvopastoral and other agroforestry systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. The runoff units from Central America are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review, entering as components of erosion, and the Costa Rica and Nicaragua figures span high- and lower-middle-income settings [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_quali.mechanism: Trees and shrubs in grazed pasture hold back nutrients that would otherwise leave the field. A global review of plot and field studies found that silvopastoral systems reduced nutrient losses from leaching, runoff and sediment by 45%, 47% and 42% on average against single pastures [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_quali.conditionality: The strong class rests on one review with no second independent source to test agreement against. Its percentages are averages of compiled study reductions rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, from temperate and tropical sites rather than low-income settings, and they measure nutrient loss at the field, a component of water-quality risk, not water quality downstream [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. Along field boundaries, on Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the cross-family, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as strong reductions, linear boundary plantings as moderate, and regeneration-based farmland and shaded perennial systems as slight. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: Two studies on rainfed cropland point to less erosion with trees. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. Neither unit gives an erosion rate, so the engine reads a slight reduction.
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: The evidence is thin and sits outside the target context. The Honduran claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning, so it cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The two units describe different practices (a slash-and-mulch field system and field shelterbelts) and different erosion processes. Missing: measured erosion rates from rainfed cropland with and without trees in low- or lower-middle-income settings.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said that planting trees in a line prevents the soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: Both units are farmer statements from Kenyan mixed crop-livestock households, gathered in interviews and focus groups during or after floods, with no measured soil loss or effect size [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee, a study on a large farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], shade trees attenuated runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3], and a review states that shade trees protect soil from erosion and conserve fertility through the leaves and branches they add [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: No unit states a size against the counterfactual (full-sun plots for coffee, unsheltered fields for shelterbelts), so the engine reads a slight reduction. The runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on these soils [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. All units are from high-income settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target: the Costa Rican units are crop-specific coffee evidence, much of it from a single farm, and the Canadian unit is temperate shelterbelt evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The Canadian unit infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. This evidence should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC systems without local evidence.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: Under silvopastoral systems in Colombia, mean erosion fell by 35.3 percent in the Coffee Ecoregion (12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha on degraded pasture) and by 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley (17.5 against 18.5 t/ha) [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. A Brazilian review explains that agroforestry increases soil cover and improves soil structure, protecting against raindrop impact and reducing wind speed and surface runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. In Chiapas, Mexico, after Hurricane Stan, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell, and roadside landslides were more numerous where complexity was lower [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: The reduction differs widely between the Colombian regions, and the comparator is degraded pasture [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Latin America, matching this scope row but not LIC/LMIC evidence, and the Brazilian unit is a review statement working through runoff, a component of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. The fodder-bank runoff comparison is a review citation without a size, and runoff is a component of erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas evidence is crop-specific coffee from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume and gives no size [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__water_quality_risk.mechanism: Trees on farms reduce the nutrients and sediment that reach water. A global review of plot and field studies found that silvopastoral systems reduced nutrient losses from leaching, runoff and sediment by 45%, 47% and 42% on average against single pastures, and that linear tree plantings decreased average nutrient loss from leaching and runoff by 16% and 33% [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1, ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates downstream siltation as decreased, its compiler noting that less wind and water erosion reduces the siltation of ponds and water pans [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].
agroforestry__water_quality_risk.conditionality: The size rests on a single review, whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, drawn from temperate and tropical sites rather than low-income settings [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1]. Nutrient and sediment losses are components of water-quality risk measured at the field edge; no unit measures water quality in streams or reservoirs. Linear plantings vary widely: the same review reports their effect on nitrogen loss ranging from an increase to a large decrease [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR siltation unit is a compiler judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].

agroforestry__water_stress.mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the two sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1], and in a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised the rainwater use efficiency of sole millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 17 % in the control and 11 % with manure or phosphate [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1], and in a Ghanaian cocoa plantation the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa raised water uptake and reduced soil water below that under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Rainfall over agricultural land can also shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].
agroforestry__water_stress.conditionality: The sub-practice rows disagree, so this roll-up states the conflict rather than a pooled direction: the meta-analysis carries the cross-family row toward less water stress, the Malawi Gliricidia trial (with the German trial) carries the planted silvoarable row the same way, the cocoa soil-water deficit, now measured directly in Ghana as well, carries the shaded-perennial row toward more water stress, the regeneration-farmland row is itself conflicting, the Faidherbia subsoil depletion set against the Honduran Quesungual soil-humidity gain, and the linear-boundary row leans slightly toward more water stress on one Canadian shelterbelt study [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The Niger rainwater use efficiency is crop biomass per mm of rainfall in a two-block trial where tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]. These units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The German result counts little: it is a temperate high-income trial whose differences were not significant at all positions, and it measured surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a soil-moisture measurement, and stays on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa units are crop-specific and do not measure crop water stress directly; in Ghana the soil-water gap was largest in the dry and El Niño periods [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.mechanism: In rainfed cropping the measured evidence points both ways. Trees draw down deeper and dry-season soil water: under Faidherbia albida parkland with wheat in Ethiopia, soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4].
