In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

No study in this cell measures crop water stress itself; soil moisture and water productivity are read as components of it. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.mechanism: Shade trees and the crop beneath them both draw on soil water, so shaded cocoa soils hold less water than full-sun cocoa. A pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found soils in cocoa agroforestry systems have a significantly lower volumetric water content than in monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In a Ghanaian cocoa plantation, the combined transpiration of the shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake and reduced soil water below that under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2].
agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.conditionality: The sources agree on the direction but neither states a size in the quoted text, so the class is a slight increase in water stress. In the Ghana study the gap was largest in the dry and extremely dry El Niño periods, when it matters most, and canopy interception under shade also lowered throughfall [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Soil moisture is a component of water stress, not a measure of crop water deficit; the meta-analysis spans many shade designs, from simple shade to complex agroforests, so the effect will vary with shade-tree species and density [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. Both units are crop-specific (cocoa) and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; the evidence is mainly from lower-middle-income producers, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.mechanism: Only two temperate field studies sit in this high-income row, and they point in opposite directions. agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.conditionality: The two units differ in practice, year and position, so they do not contradict each other directly: the German comparison is alley cropping against an open field in a drought year, while the Canadian study compares soil close to a shelterbelt with soil further into the same field [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. agroforestry__waterlogging__all.mechanism: Trees take excess water out of waterlogged soil. A review reports, second-hand, that under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, indicating greater removal of excess water from the soil and a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. A biodrainage review reports a field study by Ram et al. (2011) in canal-irrigated waterlogged fields of Haryana, India: parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis on farm boundaries, spaced at 66 m with two rows of trees at 1 × 1 m, lowered the groundwater table beneath the strips by 85 cm compared with adjacent unvegetated fields in 3 years [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].
agroforestry__waterlogging__all.conditionality: Both units are second-hand readings in reviews (the biodrainage figure is from Ram et al. 2011), both from lower-middle-income India within the LIC/LMIC target, and neither reports a yield or livelihood outcome: they show water leaving the soil (evapotranspiration, a lower water table), not that crops or incomes recovered [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9, ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1]. Neither says how big the effect on the hazard's impact is, so the strength is not quantified. The 85 cm drop was measured under the strips themselves, against unvegetated fields; how far the effect reaches into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1]. The Haryana case is a canal-irrigated system, and nothing in the evidence covers severe or extreme waterlogging.

agroforestry__wind_cyclone__agro_pastora.mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind speed over a zone that typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, and live fences in India are used as windbreaks [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. In the other direction, a Latin American adaptation review lists planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms as a case of increased vulnerability [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__wind_cyclone__agro_pastora.conditionality: The evidence splits between wind sheltering and storm damage, and the wind units concern wind erosion and sheltering rather than cyclone impacts [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. All three are reviews citing other work; only the Indian unit names a country (lower-middle income) [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

agroforestry__wind_cyclone__all.mechanism: Boundary and line plantings slow the wind: the zone of reduced wind speed typically extends 10 to 20 times tree height downwind (Tibke 1988), hedges protect sandy, poorly covered soils from wind erosion in Senegal, live fences serve as windbreaks in India, and a meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found wind speed 35.80% lower in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The evidence about trees on farms in general points both ways: a review of smallholder agroforestry notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms, while a Latin American adaptation review gives the planting of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. In hurricane-hit coffee in Soconusco, Chiapas, vegetation management had significant effects on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
agroforestry__wind_cyclone__all.conditionality: Studies disagree across sub-practices, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. The benefit side is the boundary and line plantings, which read as a moderate reduction: they slow everyday wind and wind erosion, entering as components rather than measured storm or cyclone losses [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. Against it, the shaded perennial-crop evidence shows no mitigation: after the Chiapas hurricane, coffee harvest loss did not differ with vegetation management, so shade trees did not protect the crop in that study [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The cross-cutting evidence is itself split between a smallholder review noting trees used as windbreaks and to rebuild storm-damaged property, and a Latin American adaptation review's example of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms, the one harm finding in the row [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. The separator is design and placement: a windbreak laid out to shelter a field is a different thing from shade trees over a crop or standing next to buildings when a storm hits, and no unit measures the effect in a storm the authors call severe or extreme, so the evidence does not say how far the windbreak benefit holds at storm or cyclone strength. Most units are reviews repeating earlier work. The Chinese shelterbelt result is from upper-middle-income China, and the Chiapas unit is crop-specific (coffee) from upper-middle-income Mexico, counted because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
